and eastern europe, and the european union has been involved in the negotiations with the countries of central and eastern europe. this would mean the end of convergence and the emergence of divergences fuelled by competition between countries. the context is also one of a triple asymmetry in the economic, social and demographic fields. this glaring asymmetry between the two parties to the free trade area, i.e. the union and the mediterranean countries, is also strong between the countries of the southern shore and, finally, within some of these countries, between the coastal and urbanised regions and the rural interior. in the face of all these difficulties, we need strong political will, but we must also be realistic. for this reason, and in view of the sometimes substantial delays in the implementation of the economic and political reforms necessary for the creation of a genuine euro-mediterranean market, i consider it necessary to reconsider the 2010 deadline as the genuine euro-mediterranean socioeconomic area, integrating all social and environmental issues into the economic sphere. that is why i am in favour of a free trade area which is being built in a gradual, controlled, gradual and concerted way. it must also be adapted to the socioeconomic realities of each country. the opening up of markets cannot be done at the expense of the countries of the south, taking the risk of further weakening a number of key sectors which are now sensitive and which would be due to a competitive confrontation. we all know that their agriculture is not very competitive and diversified, with a majority of small farms whose structures need to be modernised, and that it requires us to think deeply about a form of integrated agricultural policy, focused on madam president, immigration is a difficult issue in the barcelona process, it is a complex phenomenon which must be dealt with in all its dimensions and not just in its security dimension, which is too often put forward. all too often, europe has imposed the themes of the euro-mediterranean agenda, making terrorism, weapons of mass destruction, drug trafficking and immigration predominate in a kind of amalgam. we must not continue in this way: migration flows, population exchanges are an economic necessity and a human resource for the host countries. i would like to make three proposals in this connection. legal channels for immigration must be opened and illegal immigration channels, which exploit poverty and generate a new form of modern slavery, must be tackled. the political dimension of the partnership must be strengthened, as democracy, respect for fundamental freedoms, the status of women and good governance make a powerful contribution to development and also help to stem the emigration of poverty. finally, it is essential to establish operational cooperation between the authorities responsible for managing migration flows on both sides of the mediterranean, and in this respect i welcome the european initiative frontex, whose resources must be increased.
in writing. the proposed euro-mediterranean free trade area has fallen behind schedule, making completion unlikely by 2010. there is, however, an urgent need to take initiatives in this part of the world where the union should be much more present. our first priority should be, through the european neighbourhood policy, a more targeted, country-by-country approach. the fact that the interest is collective does not mean that the approach must be global. the development of tailor-made cooperation is necessary if each country is to become economically strong enough to participate in the free trade area. this cooperation must be open to the local authorities on both sides of the river, in order to establish strong links at all political levels. our second objective must be to boost south-south trade, which is still insufficient. the union has unique expertise, drawn from its enlargements, to bring to partner countries to help them prepare in key areas of their economic transition, such as education, research, training, preparation of economic and administrative actors and approximation of legislation. the euro-mediterranean free trade area can be established by supporting the creation of a genuine mediterranean common market.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank our colleagues barón crespo and guardans cambó for taking the initiative in this oral question to the commission. the issue of our trade defence instruments is a key issue, not only in ensuring effective protection of european producers against unfair forms of competition, but also in the wider debate on the place of the european union in a globalised economy and the rules it wishes to promote to regulate it. in this respect, even though the european union has always defended the multilateral wto system, it seems surprising to say the least that the commission is launching such a public consultation and is considering potentially significant reform of our defence instruments, when the wto negotiations on anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard measures have not yet been concluded and their outcome will have an impact on how these instruments will be used. i would remind the commission that it itself commissioned a study on the evaluation of european trade defence instruments and that it concluded that the status quo is both the most reasonable and the most adequate solution to address the concerns of all parties. the study also supports the view that there is clearly no urgent need at present to review or alter existing community trade defence instruments. i would therefore like to know what concrete changes the commission is planning and how parliament will be involved at all stages of this process. i therefore call on the commission to take these various elements into account, as well as the opinion of the members and the results of the public consultation it has launched for the drafting of its future proposals, in the context of the forthcoming discussions in the council.
mr president, i would like to thank the commission for initiating the debate on the union's trade defence instruments. let me congratulate my colleague, ignasi guardans cambó, on giving us the opportunity to discuss this today. what strikes me in the commission's questionnaire, or more generally in its overall thinking on trade policy, is the absence of any mention of the question of exchange rates between the euro and the currencies of our main trading partners. mr mandelson, how can you effectively defend the commercial interests of the european union with such a relationship between the euro and the dollar, the euro and the yuan and the euro and the yen? so, speaking of an industry which is now in the forefront of the scene with social plans, job cuts, threats of outsourcing or offshoring, that is to say aeronautics, a 10 cent change in the exchange rate between the euro and the dollar is equivalent to a loss or gain of one billion euros in airbus' profit. is this not the first of the dumping, the competitive devaluation of our competitors? as a result, it has become preferable for airbus, the jewel of european industry, to produce some of its aircraft outside the eurozone in order to compete with boeing. thank you for the gift! i encourage you, mr mandelson, to turn to the european central bank and to make it responsible today not just when the euro depreciates but also when it appreciates. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
in writing. the european commission has adopted a green paper to launch a public consultation on the application of the eu's trade defence instruments (tdi) in a changing global economy. this public consultation should pave the way for commission proposals to reform its trade defence instruments (anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard clauses). however, this proposed reform must be considered with caution. the european union must not act unilaterally and hastily, because any revision of its instruments cannot take place outside the legal framework of the ongoing negotiations on the multilateral disciplines concerning the idcs within the doha cycle. in addition to the need to be in line with the wto calendar, the european commission must also take into account that trade liberalization makes the idcs indispensable. the idcs are characterized by their moderate use and are in no way the safeguards of liberalism or the weapons of protectionism. they are effective regulators in restoring the conditions for fair competition in international trade markets and limiting the negative consequences of illegal practices on community industry, growth and employment in europe.

madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on the basis of article 158 of the treaty and the declaration on island regions annexed to it, the european union takes account of the handicaps and constraints faced by these regions by adopting specific measures to promote the integration of the european islands into the internal market. but francesco musotto, whom i thank for supporting my amendments in the committee on regional development, is now quite right to ask the european commission about the actual implementation of these provisions. i would like to start by saying that the concepts of ultraperiphery and insularity are quite different, whatever the links of proximity and solidarity which unite them, since the outermost regions are characterized by their remoteness from the european continent and their belonging to a geographical area which is composed, in the vast majority, of acp countries. insularity is both a geographical and cultural asset which represents a potential to be exploited in an appropriate development strategy, but also a permanent handicap which adds an additional difficulty to the competitiveness of these regions. the principle of territorial cohesion, reinforced in the regulations on the structural funds for the period 2007-2013, must aim at the polycentric integration of the territory of the union in such a way as to allow equal opportunities for all regions and their population. and beyond the measures you have mentioned, madam commissioner, i ask the commission to take greater account of the possibility offered by the the rapporteur. mr president, i have taken the initiative of this report because i am convinced that, at a time of reform of european aid, it is essential to give local authorities a central political role in development cooperation. this is an important year: in 2007, 50 percent of the world's population lives in cities, and this is obviously going to increase very quickly. local authorities are experts in all areas of local development, and the un has already recognised their central role in achieving the millennium development goals. however, in europe, our consultation ends with civil society organisations. i think that's not enough. while the involvement of civil society is necessary, particularly ngos working closely with local communities on the ground, local authorities have a specific added value. first, they are in most cases legitimately elected throughout the territory. this democratic legitimacy is an asset to enable us to advance local democracy and good governance on the ground. secondly, they have expertise in the management of public services, such as water, health, education, urban planning, waste management, environment, etc. finally, they have a territorial approach. they are familiar with the local development problems specific to each region and each community. their active involvement in european development policy would allow aid to be better distributed throughout the territory and better targeted to the specific needs of each area, whether rural, urban, maritime, mountainous, desert or other. in the light of this, my report sets out two major challenges for the future of european cooperation. i didn't come up with my strategy on my own. i spent more than four months consulting the largest international and european local authority organisations to gather their analysis. my report is in fact the fruit of these reflections. the first challenge is that we believe that local authorities must become a full-fledged political partner of the european union alongside central governments and civil society organisations. i mean by partnership the development of a structured political dialogue between the european commission and local authority associations. this dialogue must be active, both here in brussels and on the ground in the developing countries. in brussels we want the commission to set up a dialogue platform like concord, the european confederation of emergency and development ngos. in developing countries, in line with the new development instrument and the revised cotonou agreement, local governments should be involved at every stage of the development strategy, starting from the preparation of country-specific policy documents. the second challenge is that this report presents the european commission with a number of financial proposals. firstly, we believe that decentralisation should be a priority for the union and therefore that it should be a sector of financial concentration of eu aid. in many countries, decentralisation is becoming more and more profound. local authorities have more and more powers without the financial capacity to fulfil this new role. secondly, we propose that part of the budgetary support should go directly to these local authorities. indeed, our recent debate on budgetary aid has shown how problematic it can be in countries where the risks of corruption are high. decentralising budgetary support would make it possible, on the one hand, to distribute it better throughout the territory, but also to avoid concentrating it all in the same hands and thus to ensure better management of european funds. finally, we believe that the involvement of these local authorities and non-state actors is necessary if european aid is to meet the real needs of the disadvantaged. we therefore call for an increase in the budget for the thematic programme, non-state actors and local authorities. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to stress what i consider to be the main issue in our debate. our cooperation policy does not sufficiently take into account the territorial dimension of development, and as kofi annan said at the millennium summit, if the millennium goals are global, it is at the local level that we can provide the solutions. the responses are local and specific, depending on the territory. if we do not take this into account, our aid may remain concentrated in the hands of a central government and not be distributed throughout the country. the former president of benin, mr soglo, recently told me that he thought, when he was president, that aid was distributed equally across the country, but he realised, now that he is the elected mayor of cotonou, that this was not the case. i am glad that the new development instrument recognises the need to involve local governments in political dialogue. it now remains to translate this commitment into action and equip them for their new responsibilities.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mr schapira for the preparation of this report, which should be the first step in a very significant development of our development policies. in other words, i am convinced that with this text we will be able to become really more efficient. for what is the use of having generous, often general, objectives, what is the use of having substantial financial means if one does not achieve effective and efficient results? local authorities, and this is very well explained in the report by our colleague, are the operational link which can, on the ground, provide concrete answers to the problems of the citizens of these countries: problems of drinking water, health, education, public transport and social problems. among these problems, which unfortunately are many, health problems should be the most important. in the field, local authorities are best placed to look for solutions. do they have the means to provide the right answers to these various problems? rarely, because they lack either the financial means, the experience or the means to implement it. i am convinced that this text will enable us to provide the necessary financial resources and the necessary intellectual engineering. and i hope that the good practice processes that we have set up at european level with urban will be made available to all local actors. in the face of this great challenge, i also believe that the experience - which is growing - that we have acquired in the field of the structural funds, and particularly in the cities, will be a great asset. i would also like to say, as the coordinator of my group in the committee on regional development and chairman of the urban intergroup, that although 80% of the population of the european union lives in cities, urban population growth is phenomenal in all these developing countries and only local actors can really provide the right answers at local level. these good responses will be the result of new governance: the mayors of these municipalities, in particular, will have to be both operational in terms of power - the application of their legal powers - but also operational as an animator for all these issues of waste, water, health, etc., and this is where the support we will be able to provide will allow them, at the same time, to be operational thanks to their legal powers and to play fully their role as animator. commissioner, i hope that, together with our colleagues and those of the european commission, the various dgs concerned will be fully involved in the success of this operation. our countries are waiting for us to do so. we have the means to grant their wishes. the concrete results must be in line with their expectations. mr president, i would like to join in congratulating our colleague mr schapira on his excellent report. in this report, above all, he stresses the essential role that local authorities must play in development because of their proximity and their capacity for dialogue with local populations, and also because of their knowledge of the terrain. around the world, one can see that the region, whatever name is given to it, province, governorate, department, in short, the first sub-state level is being recognized as a relevant level of spatial planning and development. in many other countries, urban units are themselves organised into regions. the regions are therefore already essential partners. it should be noted, for example, that 35 million euros are given each year by french regions to french-speaking regions of the world. this is why last week in marseille a world organization of regions was created. in other words, twelve global networks bringing together regions from the five continents, irrespective of their qualities, whether francophone, peripheral, maritime or other, are being organized into a network, the forum of networks of regions of the world. they expect the european union, commissioner, to be able to access direct international financing, to be able to participate in the establishment of integrated national programmes and the european development fund, and to be entitled to programmes of their own.
in writing. it is clear that a genuine policy of cooperation with the southern and eastern mediterranean is needed to stem the flow of migrants that europe has long been unable to accommodate. it is also clear that a reasonable trade policy can be mutually beneficial on both sides of the mediterranean. but that is not what mr arif's report proposes, which is nothing more or less than the extension to north africa and part of the middle east of the european union, of its operations and policies: integrated agricultural policy, free movement of persons and goods, freedom to provide services, to name but a few areas. what's the point? we don't know for sure, because a study cited by mr arif himself predicts negative social and environmental impacts in the short and medium term. it is therefore purely out of free trade ideology, and not in the interests of the union countries, or even of the mediterranean countries, that parliament is supporting this project.
in writing. mr voggenhuber's report seeks to make all european legislation subject to the charter of fundamental rights, which is a veritable ideological catch-all, and thus to make the charter binding. that is to say, to ignore the popular rejection of the european constitution, of which the charter was part ii, and to impose a legal constraint which was not adopted by the peoples or their parliaments! and it will have three effects. legitimate the intervention of the luxembourg court in areas which are forbidden to it by the treaties themselves, such as police and judicial cooperation, which is no small paradox. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european union-wide network of information centres for the protection of the environment. how can we change, if not completely marginally, legislation implementing a 'fundamental right'? this text is very worrying: in the name of human rights, it is succeeding in organizing the violation of democracy, the treaties and the rights of the european parliament itself!
in writing. the european parliament has a very particular and partisan approach to the definition of fundamental rights. they are used to fight against individuals whom he considers undesirable, political opponents, or embarrassing governments that are not politically correct. curiously, they are never mentioned in defence of the rights of political minorities in his assembly. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in this area, the great principles of freedom of expression and equality are completely disregarded. the european parliament puts into practice the famous formula: 'do as i say, not as i do'. the european political caste is ready to do anything to impose its vision of europe, and to do so against the will of the people if necessary. the european parliament has been working hard to get the european constitution re-introduced in pieces, even though it was rejected in referendums in france and the netherlands. similarly, while the charter of fundamental rights has no binding legal value, the text proposed here is intended to make it an indispensable, or worse, a mandatory reference text for the european courts. far from being innocent, this report is dangerous to the freedoms and rights of peoples.
in writing. the european union is currently experiencing an institutional crisis. but by voting, the french people have expressed their desire for european union, but a europe that is not limited to the single market. the citizens want a europe which also confers social rights. this proposal for a methodology for the effective implementation of the european charter of fundamental rights in the commission's legislative proposals, and in particular the systematic and rigorous verification of compliance with all the fundamental rights concerned when drawing up any legislative proposal, should help to meet this desire of europe. it seems to me therefore essential to find a way of not calling into question the legally binding nature of the european charter of fundamental rights so that it can have all the weight that european citizens want it to have.
in writing. in the globalization of finance, agriculture, migration and the market, the nations of europe must have an alliance of civilization with the nations of central america. our farmers, for example, are facing problems similar to those of the peasants in mexico or the latin smes, facing the confiscation of their intellectual property, their know-how and, above all, facing their gradual elimination by a global trading system which puts our banana producers in the french antilles or the canary islands in competition with those in honduras or nicaragua, for the sole benefit of multinationals like chiquita. the need for this alliance of civilisation between europe and latin america is even more pronounced in the face of global migration. thus, if, since the 1970s, french automobile, steel and construction manufacturers had turned to latin american labour, instead of the workforce of the aurès, anatolia or kabylia, french society would have avoided the tensions of today and public budgets would have avoided heavy burdens. latin america, in alliance with europe, would find the necessary allies in international and commercial forums to defend a conception of the management of human societies and economies different from the anglo-saxon ideology of the market.
in writing. the existence of this report on the integration of the specific features and handicaps of the island regions of the european union into regional policies is in itself a demonstration that these features, if not totally hidden for years, are not being properly addressed. this is probably due to the very nature of the european union, which is a unifying and leveling-up institution. i also regret that the emphasis is not placed on the unbearable burdens that the application, or the threat of application, of european common law, particularly in the field of taxation and competition, represents for these areas. in france, the grant of the sea, the reduced vat or excise rates applicable to corsica or the overseas departments are periodically called into question and must be periodically renegotiated in brussels by the government. finally, i regret that the submersion of some european islands by the influx of illegal immigrants is treated in this report in a local and quasi-clinical manner, when this is an extremely serious problem. the abolition of internal borders and the proselytizing of immigrants in the eu are, it should be stressed, one of the major causes of this problem.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission has been closely following the situation relating to trade unions in cambodia. the murder of mr hy vuthy, who was shot dead in the early hours of 24 february while going home after a night shift in a textile factory, is the latest in a very disturbing series of attacks on trade unionists in that country. mr hy vuthy is the third official of the free trade union of workers of the kingdom of cambodia to be killed in three years. this campaign of intimidation against trade unionists is aggravated by a weak police force and judiciary, local power struggles, political interference in the judiciary, corruption and impunity. furthermore, the mix of fierce competition for membership, the low level of professionalism, political influence and a low degree of control over members have made for a tense atmosphere in some of the garment-manufacturing establishments. the commission recently raised this issue with the cambodian authorities to ask for a thorough inquiry into this murder and that appropriate and effective action be taken to follow up the results of the inquiry and bring to justice those responsible. the eu also called on the cambodian government, as a party to all major international labour organisation conventions, to abide by the commitments it has taken. the commission has also raised, and will continue to raise, the issue of the khmer rouge tribunal, and has urged the parties concerned to come to an agreement on its rules of procedure so that the trials can get under way as soon as possible. the commission is providing eur 1 million towards the costs of the tribunal. a successful khmer rouge tribunal will contribute significantly towards eliminating the climate of impunity in cambodia. as recommended by parliament in a previous resolution on cambodia, the commission has recently established a working party to deal with matters relating to cooperation in the areas of institution-building, administrative reform, legal and judicial reform, governance and human rights in order to engage constructively the cambodian authorities on these issues. i would like to assure this house that the commission, through its delegation in phnom penh and together with the missions of eu member states in cambodia, will continue to monitor the situation very closely. the international community – especially the eu – which had such a vital role in the establishment of the new cambodia, should ensure that human rights are upheld in that country.

member of the commission. mr president, the european commission has been following the evolution of the same-sex marriage (prohibition) act submitted early last year to the nigerian federal executive council. the commission shares the deep concern already expressed by international organisations, including the un, through the secretary-general’s special representative on human rights defenders, concerning the heightened level of discrimination, violation of individual rights and restriction of the right of free association that this bill would introduce, if approved. the commission equally shares the analysis by nigerian and international human rights associations concerning the potential repercussions on persons engaging, or being suspected of engaging, in same-sex relationships. the same is true for human rights defenders advocating against the negative human rights implications of this homophobic bill. the bill would put them at greater risk of arbitrary arrest, detention, torture and ill-treatment. it would also restrict and silence the action of local human rights organisations. the bill reinforces the excessively severe provisions already in place. nigeria’s criminal code punishes consensual homosexual conduct with up to 14 years’ imprisonment, while the shariah penal code adopted in 11 states in northern nigeria lays down the death penalty for livat [‘sodomy’]. the bill would also infringe a number of international human rights laws and treaties that nigeria ceded to and ratified, possibly its own constitution and key articles of the cotonou agreement. in view of the above and of the conclusions on eu relations with nigeria adopted by the general affairs and external relations council in 2003, the commission would like to confirm its readiness to contribute to the implementation of the resolution this house is about to adopt. the commission is prepared to actively participate, along with the member states, in the political dialogue foreseen under article 8 of the cotonou agreement. this political dialogue will fully address the specific issue concerning the same-sex marriage bill as well as the essential elements regarding human rights, democratic principles, the rule of law and good governance listed in article 9 of the cotonou agreement. finally, the commission encourages the european parliament to follow up last year’s visit by its former president, mr josep borrell fontelles, to the nigerian parliament, with a view to establishing a regular dialogue between the two parliaments.

the committee on economic and monetary affairs has considered it necessary to discuss supervision among the european institutions and we wished to be able to do so in the presence of the council and the commission. in the committee on economic and monetary affairs we welcome the resumption of discussions and work in both the council and the commission on crisis management in financial markets. improving the efficiency of supervision and cooperation between supervisors is a necessity. nevertheless, if we are to succeed in the end, we believe that at this stage of development and profound transformation of the financial markets, the opening of an interinstitutional debate on this subject is probably the best way forward. the committee on economic and monetary affairs has developed its analysis of the state of the european financial system and the implications of financial consolidation in many papers, notably in the report by our colleague mr joseph muscat. in this report we support the establishment of a committee of experts to study not only the implications of consolidating financial markets and institutions, financial supervision, financial stability and crisis management, but also to come up with concrete ideas on the current structures which would be reported to parliament. the interinstitutional debate taking place today is intended to signal clearly the need to open or reopen the great debate on the future of the european supervisory architecture. it is essential for the competitiveness of the financial market itself and for the stability of the financial system in the european union. let me make a few observations at this point. the first is that the financial system in europe and the world has changed profoundly. every day we are witnessing the constant transformation of markets, the innovations that are taking place, which is reflected, among other things, in the rise of hedge funds or private equities. the continuing consolidation of financial markets has led to the emergence of major players operating on a totally transnational basis. mergers and acquisitions motivated by the search for competitiveness and efficiency have increased at national, european and global levels. they became an engine. as a result, the structure of markets, the way players operate in markets has changed dramatically. this transformation has brought new challenges and new stakes. secondly, the consolidation of financial supervision structures must go hand in hand with the consolidation of the markets themselves. but sometimes it seems to be a different rhythm. in this context, it is questionable whether the current supervisory system in the european union - supervisors under very different supervisory structures with very different competences, powers and responsibilities and acting on the basis of a national mandate - is capable of ensuring good supervision of large cross-border financial groups, whether it is sustainable and whether it does not endanger the financial stability of the european system itself. thirdly, the financial system of the european union has its own peculiarities. it is distinguished by its diversity and the richness of its operators: local actors, such as community banks, and cross-border, transatlantic and global actors. it requires a robust, effective and appropriate prudential framework to meet the challenges of regional integration, globalisation, innovation and centralisation of management, while ensuring the quality of prudential supervision and the soundness and stability of the system. fourthly, improving the supervisory arrangements is in the interest of all the players: first of all in the interest of the system itself and secondly in the interest of the market players who ask us to improve the supervisory arrangements in order to facilitate their activities on all markets. i am convinced that the end user will also be interested in an improvement of the system. my fifth and final comment concerns the transatlantic challenge of european regulatory excellence. in this respect, i think it is time to make some progress. in conclusion, and in the light of these observations, we as european legislators are faced with a major challenge: to provide europe with strong and effective supervisory structures capable of ensuring proper supervision of all financial actors, whether large crossborder groups or local banks, and also capable of making supervision an element of the competitiveness of the european model on a global scale. the question is, how? should we set up this committee of sages? or should we imagine that, on an interinstitutional basis, we may have the best capacity to make the european collective intelligence work? that is in any case the message that parliament is sending today in this debate, and i thank the council and the commission for agreeing to bring it here.

the agenda calls for the report by hélène aubert, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation on organic production and labelling of organic products (com (2005) 0671 - c6-0032/2006 - 2005/0278 (cns)) (a6-0061/2007).
member of the commission. mr president, i welcome this opportunity to discuss our proposal for a new council regulation for organic production. i want to start by thanking the rapporteur, mrs aubert, and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for their efforts. the thorough work that they have been doing is a very valuable contribution to our discussions. with 160 000 organic farms and more than 6 million hectares of land in the european union, the turnover of organic products is estimated to have a value of between 13 and 14 billion euros. this tendency is on the increase, so it is indeed a very important sector. there is no doubt in my mind that this expanding sector has an essential role to play. it addresses a range of expectations on the part of the public and of consumers; expectations about food quality, care for the environment, animal welfare and opportunities for developing the countryside. it is also a sector with plenty of optimism and confidence about what the future has to bring, as i was able to see clearly during my recent visit to the biofach in nuremberg. but in order to develop and reach its full potential, the sector needs an appropriate regulatory framework, and this is actually what we are trying to achieve with our new regulation. it is therefore a very important legislative proposal, and i am pleased with the progress that we were able to make through our deliberations last year. in 2006 very intensive discussions were held on our proposal in the council and in parliament. as a result, some elements from the original proposal that proved to be very sensitive ones have now totally disappeared. this includes a prohibition on higher claims, the mutual recognition of private standards by inspection bodies, and the eu organic indication. parliament has also proposed a range of amendments in order to improve the wording of the objectives and principles of organic farming, on the indication of the origin of the products, on the explicit right to use national and private logos, on embedding of the control system in the official food and feed controls, and the reinforced guarantees on imports. these are amendments that improve the original proposal and i am therefore happy to take them on board. we have also managed to improve the emphasis of the regulation on soil fertility, soil life and soil management practices. the question of gmo and organic farming has generated a lot of debate. i have noted parliament’s wish that operators provide proof that they have taken all the necessary steps to avoid adventitious or technically unavoidable presence of gmos, and i could not agree more with that. so although these amendments present a reiteration of an existing requirement, i have decided to accept them because of the huge sensitivity of this issue. but let me also be completely clear: the threshold for adventitious presence of gmos is not, as some suggest, a de facto threshold for gmo tolerance. gmos and their derivatives remain strictly banned for use in organic production. although the commission and parliament agree on the fundamental aspects of the new regulation, there are certain issues where we have not managed to see eye to eye, and i would like to touch briefly on some of these. parliament is asking for more details, and it is clear that a lot of the detailed rules as we know them in the current regulation have been removed. but let us not forget that one of the main purposes of this proposal was to set out the basic rules more clearly and more logically. this, however, does not mean that the detailed rules that form the unique fabric of organic standards should disappear altogether. certainly not. but i believe that they are better placed in the implementing rules, and the content of these detailed rules will, as i confirmed to you earlier on, be very similar to the detailed rules that we have in the current regulation. on our wish to extend the scope to cover mass caterers, cosmetics, textiles and preserved fish, i would like to point out that we cannot take all steps in one go. we are substantially extending the scope now to wine and to aquaculture. the other sectors are still at a very early stage of the development, and i think that harmonising them could hamper their development. the current text actually provides for the possibility of looking at the issue again in 2011. linked to this, i have also noticed that you would like to see a double legal basis for this proposal. it is no secret that there is a wider discussion on the introduction of codecision for agricultural matters. this is an important issue and it is a discussion that i have clearly indicated that i welcome. but it is an issue that should be dealt with in a horizontal manner, at the proper level and in the proper context. i do not believe that it serves anyone to take an approach on a case-by-case basis. therefore i cannot accept a change to the legal basis for the new regulation on organic farming as you have proposed. finally, you propose that member states may maintain or introduce stricter national rules. that is not acceptable to me. the very purpose of this regulation is to bring about a solid harmonisation at a strict enough level, with a flexibility mechanism for exceptions. by harmonising the rules at a fairly high level, with flexibility, i think we are reaching the same end, but with a reduced risk of unequal treatment of operators in similar conditions. i am convinced that this is a way to foster a thriving internal market for organic production. i am sorry to have spoken at such length, but it is a very important issue that i wanted to address in detail.
the commission is free to speak as long as it wishes and as much as is necessary.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the situation of organic farming is rather paradoxical today. on the one hand, it is generating a growing demand because it is a mode of agriculture that creates jobs, preserves the environment, biodiversity and, ultimately, our health. on the other hand, organic farming still represents only a little over 1% of european agricultural production and a little over 3% of the useful agricultural area, which is a small amount. i think it is our responsibility to contribute to the development of organic farming in the european union. it may be a small issue in terms of quantity, but it is a huge issue in political and symbolic terms because organic farming is also a form of vanguard for a necessary reorientation of the common agricultural policy towards a much more sustainable agriculture. throughout 2006 we worked on a commission proposal which caused a lot of concern, a lot of protest and a certain amount of haste, since we were originally asked to give our opinion within two months on a proposal which was not really thorough. but i am happy to say that the work has been constructive and that there has been regular exchanges with both the commission and the council to improve the original proposal. what was the purpose of all this exchanges, all this discussion and back and forth, in the end, by the committee on agriculture of this parliament? you have recalled the essential elements. firstly, it wanted to extend the scope of this regulation to non-food products such as textiles and cosmetics, but also and above all to mass catering, because mass catering is a formidable lever for the development of organic agriculture in our countries. it would be a mistake not to use it. this is also why we want a dual legal basis - article 37 and article 95 - covering both the internal market and consumption. it seems that you have only praised our work, our contribution and, therefore, the fact that the european parliament is much more widely involved - not to mention codecision in general for agriculture, because that is another debate we have yet to have. it seems to me that if we want to continue this work, if we want members of the european parliament to really have a say in these famous decrees which will play a vital role in the application of this regulation, you should accept this double legal basis and we will continue this debate. secondly, you mentioned it, we asked for much more precise definitions of what is meant by control, certification, products authorized or not in organic farming practices, soil connection, animal condition, etc., on the basis of a text that was vague. and then you touched on the very sensitive issue of the absence of genetically modified organisms in organic farming, which must be total, like the absence of pesticides or synthetic chemicals. on the question of genetically modified organisms, we are very keen to confirm to consumers that organic farming does not contain any gmos, from seed to distribution. the current threshold of 0.9%, which is a threshold for exemption from labelling, creates confusion. we therefore believe that this issue should be reviewed in such a way that the detection threshold is chosen for both conventional and organic crops, and that all necessary measures are taken to avoid any contamination of organic crops by gmos, even accidental ones. you say that it is not possible to accept the stricter measures that the member states would take. it seems to us that the existing specifications, whether private or those of the member states, which are well known to consumers, should be allowed to continue. in any case, that is what we want and, if there is flexibility, harmonization must go upwards and not downwards, which we fear. you've given us a number of answers. i think this debate will continue, perhaps beyond tomorrow's vote. finally, i would like to conclude by saying that this regulation is not all there is to it and that it will not solve all the problems relating to organic farming. we also need much stronger support for organic farming than we have today in the framework of the common agricultural policy.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating mrs marie-hélène aubert on the excellent work she has done since the beginning of her mandate, first on the european action plan for organic food and farming and then on this proposal for a regulation. the task was not easy because the proposal undermined the strong and credible identity of organic farming. we can be satisfied with the progress made in the committee on agriculture on several points: stricter controls on the use of plant protection products, veterinary treatments and national derogations; strengthened controls on certification, including on imported products; an extension of the scope of the regulation and the maintenance of the regulatory committees. i also support the dual legal basis which would make it possible to move to codecision. however, i remain very concerned about the presence of gmos, even accidentally, in organic products. the regulation states that a product cannot be labelled 'organically produced' if it contains gmos, but it does accept a 0.9% accidental contamination threshold for gmos, which is not acceptable. i therefore ask for your support for amendments nos 170 and 171 tabled by the pse group, which call for the presence of gmos in organic products to be limited exclusively and for the term not to be used.

resources. to speak of the union's resources is to speak of its means of subsistence, but above all it is to speak of its means of undertaking and producing public policies. it is about the continuity of the european idea and the innovative policies that only europe can give us. the socialist group wants to achieve these two ambitious objectives: the continuation of the european project and political and economic innovation. the imperative for parliament is to show the member states that a europe of projects, a europe of sharing, of solidarity, is possible. this requires that we not be union are now in great need of simplification. this complex system has become incomprehensible to the european citizen and decision-maker. it's an unfair and inappropriate system. the work done in counter to our project. this is the poison of community europe. the very notion of net balance must be abolished. the rapporteur, thanks to the amendments of the committee on budgets, has emphasized present form is a legitimation of all cases of rebates. we also confirm the options in the böge report on the financial perspective. it is essential to link this revenue reform to the expenditure reform. in this context, co-financing of the cap may be considered, but without renationalisation. the first step is to denounce an unfair system and then to provide europe with resources built on sound and fair foundations. and only in the second stage does alain lamassoure propose the creation of a tax which could take various forms while preserving the fiscal sovereignty of the member states. we support the idea of a unified tax, for example, the tax on corporate profits or the ecotax, as jacques delors proposed in 1991, or a tax on financial transactions, a tax on foreign exchange transactions. in this report we do not limit the range of possibilities. we are preparing the second phase of our work. so we're taking notice of a devious system and we're taking it down. with the exception of customs duties and certain agricultural taxes, other revenue is not own resources. in conclusion, to provide the union with real resources is to increase europe's autonomy in terms of resources so that it is no longer subject to the blocking power of a state. it also means restoring budgetary coherence. the person who decides on expenditure must be responsible for revenue to the public. and it is finally to get out of the logic of returns that for years has undermined all our european projects, destroying the very idea of solidarity, which is the foundation of europe, of which we are celebrating its 50th anniversary.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague mr thomas ulmer on the amendment of various directives on medical devices. the term 'medical devices' covers a wide range of products covering syringes, eyeglasses, devices for diagnosing diseases, small implantable devices, medical imaging etc., and it became essential to strengthen the competitiveness and medical safety in this sector. to do this, the current legislative framework, which, with three directives, defines the essential requirements to be met by medical devices, needed to be improved, in particular in terms of clinical evaluation, transparency, market surveillance, conformity of tailor-made devices, use of human tissues, coordination of independent bodies, among others. the practical provisions voted in this text will improve the harmonisation of this highly complex and diverse sector by providing clearer and simpler rules. it should be remembered that many manufacturers in this sector operate on the world market and therefore efforts will have to be made to encourage the process of international cooperation, particularly in the area of harmonization of standards.
in writing. i voted in favour of this revision. it is regrettable that the proposal to ban all carcinogens, mutagens and substances toxic to reproduction in medical devices has been rejected. nevertheless, this compromise is a crucial first step towards the elimination of toxic chemicals used in medical devices and found in the bodies of patients. the legislation will require medical device manufacturers to label devices if they contain phthalates, a family of chemicals used to make plastic flexible. the european union has classified dehp phthalate as toxic to human reproduction and there are considerable concerns about its migration from devices to patients, including infants and dialysis patients. the labelling of devices will alert doctors to the risks of exposure of their patients, and hospital purchasing managers will be able to easily identify dehp-free plastic devices already on the market. for sensitive patients, manufacturers will have to provide explanations of the risks of using devices containing toxic chemicals and suggest precautions.

in writing. i voted in favour of referring the aubert report on organic production and labelling to the committee on agriculture. it is necessary that the threshold for accidental contamination with gmos should not be the same as that for conventional agriculture, i.e. in the order of 0.9%, because this would de facto mean that contamination could no longer be prevented, nor could it be guaranteed that a product, even if certified organic, is free from gmos. in this respect, i supported the proposal from the european socialists that the presence of gmos in organic products should be limited exclusively to unpredictable and technically unavoidable volumes up to a maximum value of 0.1% and that the term organic should not be used to designate products with an accidental contamination of gmos above the detectable threshold of 0.1%. finally, i support the request for a change of legal basis on the issue of organic farming. the european parliament is moving from being a consultant to being a co-decision-maker on this issue, which is a step forward.

in writing. unlike the ecsc, which was financed by a genuine own resource, the european union having almost abandoned the collection of customs duties which now represent only 9.8% of its resources, the financing of the european budget is that of a common intergovernmental organization financed by state contributions: in this case, a gni contribution representing 73.8% of community resources. the resources are currently capped at 1.24% of gni and will remain so. it is simply foreseen that after 2014 a new system would apply, inspired by the classic federal solution of sharing the tax revenue of a tax between the union and the national states. twelve taxes are proposed for this sharing: from vat to the tobin tax and from corporation tax to eco-taxation. this is the french system from 1791 to 1917, on the additional pennies to state taxes to finance local governments. if the union were to pursue a major policy of investment in health, research, universities and railways instead of the malthusianism of article 104c of the maastricht treaty, the accession of national citizens would allow either financing by borrowing or even an allocated tax on which the profits of companies would be the right base.

member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs, and in particular the rapporteur, jean-paul gauzès, for their excellent work in preparing the report on the directive on payment services in the internal market. i also thank you for your patience regarding the deferral of this plenary vote. this has provided the time needed to find common ground between the three institutions. currently, 27 different sets of national rules apply to payment transactions. although we have the euro, national payments markets continue to be fragmented and, sadly, all too often payments are slow and expensive and consumers poorly served. this makes life for our citizens and businesses more difficult than it should be. it holds up their daily activities and hinders their business development. in some cases, desirable payment products, such as direct debits, are simply not available. the directive aims to remedy this situation in two main ways: on the one hand, by providing greater legal certainty and improved consumer protection, and, on the other hand, by opening up the payments market to more competition to encourage greater efficiency and innovation. the directive provides greater legal certainty by establishing a harmonised set of rights and obligations for users and providers, as well as clear information requirements. both are essential to an integrated eu payments market, at the heart of which is sepa, the single european payments area. sepa is an industry initiative strongly supported by the european institutions. sepa will allow for the creation of an integrated market, enabling payments to be executed more quickly and easily throughout the european union. the efficiency of our payments systems should be enhanced and the cost of payments to the economy as a whole reduced. adoption of the proposed directive is therefore crucial for the successful launch of sepa. but the picture would not be complete without the other objective of the directive, namely that of fostering more competition in payments markets through the establishment of an appropriate and balanced prudential framework for new entrants. new payment institutions, such as money remitters, mobile operators and retailers, should act as a spur to innovation. throughout these long months of negotiation, both the council and the commission have been very aware of the views set out in the report adopted by the economic and monetary affairs committee last september. the compromise text, which is now on the table as amendment 286, therefore seeks to meet these objectives and, in particular, calls for a strengthened prudential framework for the new payment institutions. in addition to the qualitative prudential requirements already proposed by the commission, these new institutions will now be subject to a regime of appropriate and balanced capital charges – both initial and ongoing, and hybrid institutions, such as retailers or telecom companies, must also meet safeguarding requirements such as ring-fencing. the directive’s scope will be limited to payments that both originate and end in the european union. it is, however, important not to forget about payment transactions involving non-eu member states or non-eu currencies. consumers rightly expect the provisions protecting them with regard to theft, loss or misappropriation of payment instruments to apply irrespective of whether non-authorised use takes place inside or outside the european union. performance, quality and price of payments made towards third countries should also improve. eu consumers transfer considerable amounts of funds to third countries, often to support their families. the costs of such payments can be very high. therefore, after three years of operation, the scope of the directive should be reviewed in order to assess whether ‘one-leg payments’, where only one of the parties involved is in the eu, or payments in non-eu currencies, should be included. let me conclude: european citizens and businesses today need a single payments market, in which payments can be made as quickly, efficiently and conveniently as domestic payments. this directive can provide the market with the necessary legal foundation for sepa and with a new prudential framework fostering new competition.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on 1 december 2005, the european commission published a proposal for a directive on payment services in the internal market with the aim of creating a genuine single market for payments in the european union. as rapporteur for parliament in january 2006, i felt that, although some of the european commission's forecasts seemed optimistic, the achievement of such a market through harmonisation of national legislation would remove some obstacles and have a positive effect on growth. i therefore approved the european commission's initiative in principle. the proposal for a directive also came at an opportune time to make the banking sector's initiative to create a single area for payments in euro a success. the objectives set out by the european commission were to strengthen competition by creating new players - as you have just mentioned, commissioner - to improve market transparency for both providers and users, and to clarify the rights and obligations of users and providers. in order to make this legislative proposal more effective and to take account of the technical constraints of industry, while maintaining the objective of reducing costs for the benefit of users, the economic committee adopted a number of consistent amendments which were finally unanimously approved by the members of the committee. throughout the procedure, informal contacts were maintained between representatives of the european parliament, the successive presidencies and the european commission. these discussions enabled parliament, which, as is rare, took its position before the council reached an agreement, to exert tangible influence on the negotiations in the council. i am particularly pleased with the fruitful cooperation with the german presidency, which has spared no effort, and with your commission. on 27 march 2007, the finance ministers meeting in the economic and financial affairs council finally adopted unanimously a general approach on a compromise text. i think that compromise is acceptable today. i would like to thank the german presidency. his efficient work and good cooperation with the european parliament have brought this matter to the point where it is now close to being settled. the council agreed with parliament on the main points, namely the reduction of the scope of application to payments in euro or other currencies within the european union - an arrangement that could be introduced after a trial period - the restriction of the activity of payment institution to legal persons, the introduction of strict conditions for authorisation, the introduction of initial and ongoing capital, the limitation of funds for hybrid institutions, the limitation of the granting of credit to twelve months with the prohibition of revolving credit, and the introduction of a provision indicating that the granting of credit must not be in contradiction with european and national rules, in particular those relating to consumer credit. the commission has also made progress in the areas of better information for consumers, by distinguishing between information which must be actively provided and information which must only be made available to consumers, the possibility for micro-enterprises to benefit from the same protection as consumers with regard to information, and a limited possibility of derogation, with a maximum transaction volume of eur 3 million. the text as it stands sets a deadline for execution at j+1 and a clear division of responsibilities between the different payment service providers in the event of a transaction being executed incorrectly. this is the compromise text on which parliament will vote tomorrow. given the significant progress made at ecofin towards parliament's position and the stakeholders' objective of reaching agreement at first reading, i tabled only one amendment in plenary, which takes up the ecofin compromise. i would ask my colleagues to support this amendment. an amendment 287 on data protection, which aims to amend article 71, was tabled by the european unitary left. i do not think that this amendment should be accepted by parliament. on the other hand, commissioner, it would be desirable - and i am also addressing the representatives of the presidency and the council - that parliament should be given assurances in this respect. the compromise text is certainly not perfect and some of my colleagues may have the opportunity to say so. however, it has the merit of laying the already solid foundations for an internal payments market. it is important to stress what this step forward represents, which leads to the harmonization of payment systems which are now strictly national. it is worth noting that this is not just the case for crossborder payments, which account for less than 5% of payments, but for all payments made. despite its obvious technical aspect, this text has a certain political significance. it improves the relationship between consumers and payment financial service providers and participates in the lisbon strategy. but i would also like to emphasize that on this specific and particularly sensitive subject, since it could create conflicts of interest, parliament, in its diversity, has found a solution more quickly than the governments. maybe it's because we have more here than elsewhere... the rapporteur. madam president, mr vice-president of the commission, mr jacques barrot, ladies and gentlemen, i will begin by saying that port state control is a key element of maritime safety, because it is preventive and it makes it possible to detect the main anomalies on board a ship. in addition, we europeans carry out very thorough checks in accordance with our standards, regardless of the flag of the ship, which gives it a high degree of reliability. the directive we are working on dates back to 2001 and made it possible to impose on member states an obligation to check 25% of the vessels calling at their ports. to reach this figure, checks are too often carried out on ships in good condition; the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to grant exemptions from the general rules on the protection of the environment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the most dangerous vessels are inspected first. this is the strong and new element of the inspection regime that i support: to inspect 100% of the vessels, depending on the risk they actually represent. i propose that inspections be modulated according to the risk profile to be established for each ship. three profiles should be used: low, normal or high, a result established from parameters defined in the report. these risk profiles will determine the intervals between inspections, which may not exceed six months for high risk ships. and the scope of the inspections is again detailed in the report. our objective is simple but clear: to eradicate the polluting garbage ships. to this end, we are proposing more coercive measures to hold maritime transport actors to account. the text therefore provides for stronger measures, such as the refusal of access to port and anchorage for dangerous vessels, and introduces the permanent ban on certain dangerous vessels. i would like to make it clear that we want shipping companies to respect european rules. today, some are still too neglectful; this is one of the reasons why we are proposing to establish a blacklist of low-performing companies, which will be published on the internet. i would like to stress, however, that there has been a broad convergence of views on all these proposals, even though the report is much more ambitious than it was originally. we have decided, with the support of the european commission - which i would like to thank for its work - to move to a higher speed, so that our control system remains an example at international level. that is why we must accept the rules adopted in the paris memorandum of understanding, in order to strengthen the european union's position in negotiations with other states, in particular russia and canada. the council has for the gue/ngl group madam president, the transport sector is vital to the development of our societies. in this sector, shipping is gaining momentum every year and could bring real environmental and economic improvement. however, for the last thirty years, shipwrecks of ships laden with crude oil, heavy fuel or chemicals have been increasing off the eu coast, with dramatic consequences for economic and leisure activities linked to the sea such as fishing, oyster farming, tourism, yachting and many others. a shipwreck occurs every three days. 1,600 sailors go missing at sea every year. more than 6,000 ships officially classified as dangerous are sailing the oceans every day. this is unacceptable! serious action requires a vigorous tackling of the root cause of maritime insecurity. the flags of convenience and the tax havens that shelter and protect them, the criminal complicity between the classification societies and the insurance companies, are what are responsible for the garbage ships, served by crews of sailors reduced to a state of virtual slavery. in view of this, inspections in union ports should cover not only the condition of the vessels but also the situation of the crews, in order to verify that their training, working conditions, remuneration and health are compatible with the safety requirements for navigation. commissioner, madam president-in-office of the council, would you board an aircraft whose crew is unable to communicate in a common language, whose pilot has not been paid for three months and whose co-pilot has not had a rest period for six months? of course not! then why accept it for a ship? another important point is that the creation of an independent authority to take the place of the member states in managing maritime crisis situations is inadequate, inefficient, dangerous and undemocratic. the record of most of the independent authorities in the union, starting with the ecb, is so disastrous for all the peoples of europe that i would not leave the responsibility for maritime security off my city of calais to a pseudo-independent body whose sole purpose is, as usual, to protect the financial interests of a few large companies. the last point: it concerns the fitting out of fishing vessels with an anti-collision system, at a cost of eur 2 000. could this cost be borne by the charterers and in particular by the charterers of oil tankers?
on behalf of the its group. madam president, commissioner jacques barrot, colleagues, as a french elected representative of the large north-west region, a region with many maritime facades, i am naturally concerned about maritime safety issues. i therefore fully support the commission's initiative to create, on the basis of a body of legislation, a defence mechanism to protect europe from the risks of pollution and accidents at sea. in fact, despite the progress made since the erika and prestige disasters - with, for example, compulsory inspections of ships in ports or the disappearance of single-hull oil tankers - i think that the accident prevention system is still insufficient. this sad fact is unfortunately shared by the seafarers' trade unions, environmental associations and elected officials of all stripes. this is particularly the case with the complacency flags, which, despite the desire of the commission and this parliament to reform them, are still far too numerous. almost 60% of the world fleet is still sailing under a free flag, which offers, in addition to the benefit of minimal taxation, the possibility of multiplying intermediaries in order to escape any liability in the event of an accident or disaster. it also allows the greatest laxity in matters of ship safety and labour law. finally, maritime safety should obviously be based on a trio of responsibilities: that of the flag state, that of the shipowner and that of the so-called classification societies, which are responsible for the expertise of the vessels. such measures are certainly included in the third maritime safety package. but we hope that they will be implemented, which is unfortunately not always the case.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i myself happened to be the rapporteur for the first part of this maritime package at the last partsession in march, since we had decided to discuss martha vincenzi's report on the state of the flag and my report on civil liability. i think it is very important to reaffirm today that this is indeed a comprehensive package and to send the message to the council that it must not play the horace and the curiace. we want to remain very consistent, and i hope we will succeed, because this package is a set of extremely important and particularly exemplary texts. we shall be discussing texts on maritime safety in cold weather, i.e. outside the pressure of catastrophic events. i have experienced the two preceding ones, here in this house, either with the erika or with the prestige. i have also experienced the sometimes hypocritical interpellation of the member states pointing out the shortcomings of europe: but what is europe doing? it is europe's fault that there is so much imprudence, it is europe's fault that ships are allowed to sail in this state, it is europe's fault that it is unable to compensate for the resulting ecological disasters. if we are going to complete the exercise to which we are invited today, it will not be europe's fault but the fault of the member states, whose first two packages have shown that when they are told that they are "lacking" in legislation, they are much less enthusiastic and the application of the texts is much more laborious. so we have a package of seven particularly coherent pieces of legislation in a european maritime environment which is, it must be said, probably one of the most fragile and risky in the world. we have a complicated geography and areas of risk: the calais strait - the increase in traffic in the calais strait has created and continues to create major accidents - the baltic and the sound, the bosphorus, not to mention gibraltar. we are also one of the world's leading maritime powers, probably the first, although china is now overtaking us. it is therefore absolutely essential that we have a strong legal framework to protect europe and to send a signal to everyone that we have security requirements and that these requirements are first and foremost preventive. we do not want to make shipowners pay for their mistakes and make them pay for them, but we want shipowners, like all shipping operators, to be much more cautious and to know that they will be put under pressure by their insurers, by all the partners, so that they are extremely rigorous and take as little risk as possible. the accident will always exist, but i think we will be proud of having done our utmost, while remaining within the framework of the international law of the international maritime organization, to have a european area of exemplary maritime law.
the president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. thank you for an interesting debate. the importance of safety regulations in the maritime sector has been emphasized by consensus. the rapporteur has also stressed this importance, not only in connection with the recent shipwreck in greece, but in the past. so the question is how we can improve prevention and act sensibly in an accident situation. before i go into the details, i should like to say that on the one hand i fully understand that parliament is here to discuss all the proposals together and perhaps to decide on them. on the other hand, we are moving at very different speeds in the council with regard to the agreement on the individual proposals for directives. perhaps we should adopt a pragmatic approach here too, by deciding in the council what is ready for adoption with the consent of the european parliament and adopting at a later date what is still to be regulated. this would be a sensible guideline if we want to make progress in the field of security, perhaps also in the council, under the slogan 'doing what is possible and acting pragmatically'. i would like to make a few points, particularly on the subject of control of ships, which has been discussed at length here. i would point out that the paris memorandum of understanding provides for the abolition of controls on 25% of vessels and therefore includes a risk approach. this risk approach is naturally related to and classified by the risks associated with the vessels. the approach proposed in the paris memorandum of understanding is therefore very close to your ideas. the most important thing is that this memorandum of understanding also includes russia and canada. one of the last speakers referred to the baltic sea. that is why it is very important that the russian nation state should support this declaration of intent. the second point concerns the emergency shelters. this subject has also been discussed at length here. the question of what an independent authority is and how the allocation will be made is certainly a question of finding a pragmatic solution. the question of jurisdiction needs to be clarified. however, there is also a broad consensus that emergency berths must be available everywhere. the question is how they are documented and published. we will be able to solve this together, because there are no differences in substance, but only in the question of who is in charge of what. this must be discussed with the member states. the question is also how we can ensure that there is an independent institution and thus an independent inquiry into maritime accidents. we shall certainly make progress in this area too under the presidency. it is reasonable and necessary to make an independent decision on the investigation and the differentiated publication of the results. it has been pointed out - and i very much support this - that the issue of maritime safety is not just about technical standards - about monitoring and intelligence systems - but also about the quality of work on board ships. i therefore stressed at the beginning of my speech that the ilo maritime labour convention is very important to us. the implementation of this working agreement is an important form of quality assurance on board, because it is not only a question of ensuring that the workers who work there have a certain qualification, but also that the quality of the work of the people ensures safety on board. this is also an important safety aspect which is not covered in this package but is supplemented elsewhere in this package. i am therefore pleased that we are making progress in the individual member states of the european union, particularly in connection with this maritime labour convention, to ensure a rapid implementation of the ilo minimum standards, which are applicable worldwide and therefore also to ships calling at a european port. all in all, this was a very important debate. they will decide on each proposal in the next few days and we shall see how far we can get closer. i hope that we can deal with this package and the other dossiers which are not yet on the council's agenda soon. i believe that we are all committed to setting the signals for safety on the high seas by june, in the context of the council presidency.

it is up to the member states to set up such bodies at national level. what we care about is their independence. in amendments nos 31, 32 and 33 you suggest a slightly different presentation of two basic principles. first, that ships in distress be accommodated in a place of refuge. the refusal is possible, but it must remain the exception, based on an objective assessment of the situation, on the effect of reducing compensation paid to victims and creating disparate systems coexisting in the union will be excluded. i also support amendments nos 13, 14, 15 which provide for the gradual
