the rapporteur. mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the completion and proper functioning of our internal market today requires that economic operators be given greater access to the union's territory. in this context, european companies must be sure that in the event of problems they will have a legal framework to protect their interests. in the field of public procurement, they must in particular be guaranteed that they will be able to bring effective actions if they consider that their rights have been infringed during the award of such contracts. national legal systems already provide for a number of provisions to this effect. however, the absence of coordinated rules on time limits for pre-contractual remedies has contributed to a race to the signing of contracts, which has the effect of preventing any challenge to the procedures initiated after the contract has been signed. the main objective of the text on which parliament is called upon to give its opinion today in plenary, which is the result of the compromise reached with the european commission and the council, is to solve this problem. i would like to thank the fictitious rapporteurs of the various political groups for their excellent cooperation in a spirit of openness and dialogue. i would also like to thank the representatives of the commission and the council presidency for their availability, expertise and willingness to reach an agreement at first reading. the final text confirms the general orientation of the reform around two main objectives: firstly, to preserve the applicants' rights of appeal by providing for the timely suspension of the contract; the commission has also proposed that the council should establish a set of appropriate sanctions to prevent abuses. to achieve the first objective, parliament, the commission and the council propose the introduction of a minimum suspensive period of 10 days, or 15 days in certain cases, between the decision to award the contract and the signing of the contract, in order to allow the time necessary for the applicants who consider themselves unfairly treated to lodge an appeal. in order to take account of the realities on the ground, this minimum period will not apply to a number of situations, in particular in cases of imperative urgency. the specific situations linked to the framework agreements will also make it possible to derogate from this suspensive period, subject to particularly exemplary sanctions if irregularities are found. the second major axis of the reform project concerns the penalties for breaches of the rules. the compromise reached with the council and the commission on this issue fully reflects the concern expressed by parliament to have a range of sanctions that are both severe and adapted to the realities faced by local authorities. thus, serious breaches of the rules will lead to the nullity of the contract, creating a deterrent effect vis-à-vis the contracting authorities. among these cases are illegal over-the-counter contracts, which the court of justice has considered to be the most serious breach of the rules applicable to public procurement. infringements of the rules on framework agreements and infringements which affect the chances of tenderers to obtain the contract are also concerned. the cancellation of contracts will not, however, be compulsory in cases of minor infringements, the draft reform leaving the possibility of applying other, less drastic sanctions. it will also be possible to derogate from the principle of nullity if there are overriding reasons of general interest which require that contracts be maintained in force, subject, of course, to safeguards which parliament has requested and obtained. the draft reform submitted to the vote by the members is a balanced text, based on these two objectives, and has been approved by the representatives of parliament, the commission and the council. finalised within a tight timetable, it offers a set of guarantees which are necessary for economic operators applying for public contracts, without imposing excessive constraints on the contracting authority. the adoption of this directive today will enable europe to take a further step towards harmonizing the rules governing its internal market. it will also help to equip the union with effective tools to make public procurement practices more ethical by reducing the risks of fraud and corruption.
mr president, this is a text which, from a technical and legal point of view, is of great practical importance, since it is in fact a question of preserving the possibilities of appeal of candidates for a public contract by introducing a period of suspension of the award of the contract, namely a period between the award of the contract and the signing of the contract, so as to allow unfortunate candidates to bring an action, knowing that it is much more useful to try to challenge the signing of a contract than to obtain damages and interest once the contract has been signed. the proposal also provides for effective measures to combat the illegal award of over-the-counter contracts. the discussion with the council was based on mr fruteau's excellent report, mainly on the question of the sanction to cancel contracts which would have been awarded in breach of the suspension period, which we achieved at the end of the trilogue. the member states are thus able to provide for alternative sanctions for breaches of the standstill period or the suspensive period, and we support this proposal. it's a good compromise. the annulment penalty for infringements and the possibility of applying other sanctions, and thus leaving a certain margin of manoeuvre to the national courts in the event of a breach of the suspension period, is a good formula and we approve of it.

least possible cost. unbundling is the instrument that guarantees that investments are being met and consumers are protected. i think this is a point of departure for the issues that have been debated vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, while i am grateful to all those who have spoken, including the rapporteur, i am afraid i have some reservations about accepting the somewhat restrictive approach that the committee on transport has wished to adopt. as some honourable members have rightly said, most recently mr segelström and others, to limit the minimum threshold for the definition of a european infrastructure to three or more countries would, in my view, have two drawbacks, the first of which would be to prevent the smallest european countries from participating in the programme for the protection of critical infrastructure. we obviously want to avoid such an eventuality. we want to offer all member states which are potential targets of a terrorist attack a form of participation in this european strategy. i would like to raise a few objections to the restrictive approach which is hostile to the idea of europe dealing with a common framework for the protection of infrastructure. it is not a question of subsidiarity, which we respect very much. the problem is that today's infrastructures are intimately connected and the latest speech by the representative of estonia, who recalled the cyber attack on her country, is the most obvious proof of this: it was an attack on an entire country system. and even though it only affected one country-system, can we have any doubt that that attack indirectly affected the entire network of relations of estonia with other european countries? if you paralyse the banking system of even one country for a number of days, you inevitably hit a backbone of the european union. i therefore believe that the original commission proposal, which i support, is better because it offers a wider range of opportunities. with reference to cyber attacks, i do not exclude that terrorists may plan an attack on a country-system, a banking system, a ministry, a system of administrations: we're looking into what happened in estonia and our cybersecurity agency will give us a report after the summer. i intend to publish that report, but beyond the analysis of that incident, we cannot rule out that terrorist organizations are planning to attack an entire country with a cyber attack. i think that is why a somewhat less restrictive interpretation is absolutely necessary. in conclusion, i would like to thank the rapporteur and all the members of this parliament once again. i believe that the adoption of a rigorous report on the initiatives taken by the commission would also make it clear that we are concerned about prevention. as has been rightly stated, since 2004 the european commission and the institutions of the european union have been working to strengthen prevention policies. only then will we be able to give a truly serious and coordinated response to the threat of terrorism.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, while many of us agree that the full opening up of postal services to competition in 2010 will encourage the design of services with a european dimension and will have a strong impact on job creation, there are also many of us who say that this modernisation of the postal sector must not undermine the current quality of postal services, which are part of the economic and social life of all our territories, and particularly the most remote ones. i had already expressed this in february 2006, recalling the legitimate fears of our citizens, postal employees and long-standing operators. and i know that some fears remain in the minds. since then, the work of parliament, with its different sensitivities, has allowed for greater flexibility in the definition of universal service and its financing, in particular through the introduction of the compensation fund which makes it possible to distribute the cost of the service fairly among operators, depending on whether they participate in the exercise of this service in whole or in part. while we are closely monitoring the implementation by the authorities of the various countries, and in particular my own, of an ambitious definition of universal service, we will be very attentive to its financing mechanisms which make it possible to have a quality postal service for all our territories, and above all for citizens, for employees, but above all for european citizens as a whole.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, competition has its virtues, but in a market economy, before we can let it go, we have to do a lot. as such, land use planning is one of the conditions for attractiveness, economic efficiency and quality of life. the full privatisation of the postal service may undermine this territorial planning and, therefore, the good of nations. france is not a flat country with a homogeneous topology. the cost of delivering the letter varies widely from place to place. privatizing the service means that sooner or later it will be charged at the actual cost or abandoned. as a result, rural or remote areas, already threatened by economic desertification, will suffer a competitive disadvantage that will push them into the deflationary spiral. we must therefore, in this house, once again admit that our countries are different in nature and culture. so each of them must be given the sovereign freedom to find the solution that suits them. the internal market is not an end in itself, it is only a tool for the good of nations. let us not forget this for the sake of our fellow citizens!
mr president, i should like to begin by apologising to you for the delay in bordeaux of my colleague gilles savary. as the future of the public postal service is being decided, i would like to stress one particular point: the financing of the universal service. what is being proposed today is to replace what remains of the residual monopoly which is used to finance universal service in a simple and transparent way with a range of complex and opaque systems whose only merit would be to guarantee free and undistorted competition in the postal sector. this palette includes compensation funds which are known to open the door to permanent litigation, public subsidies which portend proceedings against member states or a so-called 'pay or play' system which has never been tried and which, too, is likely to open the door to permanent challenges. the gas plant we want to set up is the result of a purely ideological choice, which has nothing to do with the real efficiency and quality of the postal service. in the long term, this system will lead to a gradual reduction in the scope of the universal service and the end of the single tariff, while having a certain impact on employment and administrative costs. we cannot support that. the postal service, especially in rural areas, is not just a commercial service, but a tool for social and territorial cohesion, and dismantling it will not reconcile europe with its citizens.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague jan mulder on the reduction, to a minimum, of administrative expenditure imposed by european legislation. the european commission's objective of better lawmaking must be encouraged and monitored. unnecessary administrative expenditure is the scourge of our rule-of-law societies, which sometimes fail to realise that inflation of the law leads to its depreciation, because citizens do not apply unnecessary and costly rules. it is not an illusion to envisage a 25% reduction in administrative expenditure by 2013, provided that we analyse what this is all about and do not lose sight of the fact that false savings can cost much more. everyone knows that mediocrity is much more expensive in the long run than quality. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague diana wallis on the joint proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the law applicable to non-contractual obligations (rome ii). this extremely complex matter is a step towards harmonizing national rules on the conflict of laws applicable to non-contractual obligations, i.e. the consequences of road accidents, unfair competition, environmental damage, defamation and, more generally, violations of personality rights, etc. the european parliament has not been heard sufficiently by the member states and the many studies and reports which will have to be produced to assess the consequences of this agreement will be essential to reviewing this important matter. for example, in the case of road accidents, how can we simply apply the law of the place of the accident, and not that of the victim's domicile, and can we be sure that the mere recitals of this regulation will oblige the courts to calculate the damage? how are we going to deal with libel in an internationalized and dematerialized press? and there are others... we have a lot of work to do on these issues.
in writing. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the balanced text she has proposed to us. the purpose of this text is to establish a coherent legal framework for the relationship between private international law and other community instruments. the purpose of the rome ii regulation is to harmonize national rules on the conflict of laws. these rules determine the law applicable to non-contractual obligations such as, for example, road traffic accidents, product liability, unfair competition or environmental damage. we are in favour of the very principle of adopting standard rules on the conflict of laws, but we must remember that they must be sufficiently clear and precise. this was not the case with the controversial provisions on media defamation. freedom of expression and of the press must be protected and fully exercised. in the absence of rules protecting editorial independence, it was reasonable to exclude the provisions on the violation of privacy by the media from the scope of rome ii. we shall therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of the compromise negotiated with the council on the second programme of community action in the field of health 2007-2013. the european union can no longer save a common health programme with a common public investment. it is regrettable that the budget has been revised downwards. a large number of investments are necessary before preventive and technical means can be provided. prevention is better than cure, so good information on healthy lifestyles or diets is a necessary prerequisite to reduce deaths from serious diseases. technical solutions for emergency situations must also be generalised. the widespread availability of defibrillators is one example among many. but health is not just a matter of accounting. it is also, and above all, a good for all. empowering patients is a central element. clear and applicable provisions throughout the union are undoubtedly the most necessary way forward.
in writing. i welcome the council's wise decision on the common position, which incorporates most of the amendments adopted by the european parliament. the main difference between parliament's and the council's position concerns mercury barometers and the derogations to be introduced, on the understanding that the ban which would then apply would only apply to new mercury barometers, as barometers already in circulation can still be resold, repaired and maintained. in view of the very dangerous properties of mercury and the very high mercury content of conventional barometers compared, for example, to medical thermometers, the limited derogation solution proposed by the council is a balanced compromise: it is a temporary derogation to allow manufacturers of conventional barometers to adapt to the new situation.
in writing. i would like to welcome the adoption of the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 76/769/eec on the restriction of the placing on the market of certain measuring devices containing mercury. i am in favour of limiting the placing on the market for the general public of measuring devices containing mercury, which have been banned in france since 1998. the council's common position, accepted by parliament, strikes a balance between reducing the release of mercury into the environment and providing for a transitional period for certain items such as traditional barometers. a transitional period of two years after the date of entry into force of the directive will allow the industries concerned to move their technology towards mercury-free devices.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my swedish colleague, åsa westlund, on food additives. while it is right to facilitate the european commission's task by accepting that decisions on the authorization of food additives fall within the committee procedure, the commission must take account of the remarks which parliament has made repeatedly over the years in the new regulation on food additives, as well as in the new regulation establishing a uniform authorization procedure for food additives, enzymes and flavourings. these comments concern mainly the environment, public health and people with allergies. it is good that the current legislation provides that the authorization of additives cannot mislead the consumer. however, coloring agents may be used to make a food appear to contain fruit when it does not. consumer protection must therefore be strengthened in this respect without prejudice to industrialists.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my irish colleague, avril doyle, on the proposal for a parliament and council regulation on food enzymes, amending many existing texts. in order to remove barriers to trade and to avoid legal uncertainty, as well as divergence in health and consumer protection standards between member states, it is urgent to harmonise at community level the rules on the use of enzymes in the food processing sector, which has developed considerably in recent years (bread, cheese, beer, fruit juice, starch processing, etc.). the great scientific and technological developments, which make it possible to obtain new enzymes from genetically modified micro-organisms, must lead us to accept this prospect of harmonizing legislation on the use of food enzymes in the european union. this is in the best interests of consumers and industry, provided that legislation is not too costly.
in writing. i voted in favour of the very good report by my slovenian colleague, mojca drčar murko, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on flavourings and certain food ingredients with flavouring properties intended for use in and on food and amending many existing texts. at present, all natural tastes and smells can be reproduced by a synthetic process from 2600 molecules with flavouring properties, with the possibility of creating new tastes that do not exist in the natural state. technological developments in the flavour sector and the volatility of tastes among our citizens must commit us to food safety and consumer protection, while offering the industry concerned the opportunity to pursue technological development, and at the same time helping to strengthen the internal market. there are many questions, and i welcome the compromise reached by the rapporteur, which makes the proposal for a regulation an effective initiative to modernise and simplify legislation on flavourings.
in writing. i voted in favour of the package on the rationalisation of authorisation procedures, the use and consolidation of the directives on additives and flavourings, and the harmonisation of legislation on enzymes. a number of additional safeguards have been introduced to ensure transparency of decisions and consumer protection, and i welcome this. the future legislation will aim to ensure consumer protection and food safety while preserving innovation and the competitiveness of the agri-food industry. the food industry uses many natural and artificial flavourings: as many as 2,600 are listed. more and more enzymes are also used in the manufacture of foodstuffs and legislation has been adopted to improve the safety of these substances. the competitiveness of the agri-food industry on the market should therefore be preserved. natural flavourings are composed entirely of natural flavouring agents. the 90/10 ratio proposed by the commission made it possible to obtain a natural flavour with different tastes depending on the products, the targets or the culture of the member states. 10% was from natural sources other than the substance concerned. i therefore regret the adoption of the arbitrary so-called 95/5 rule which risks penalizing the agri-food industry without, however, strengthening consumer information.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my dutch colleague jeanine hennis-plasschaert on the proposal for a council directive on critical infrastructure. first of all, i welcome the vision of the european council of june 2004 which is the basis for this proposal for a directive. it is imperative that the european union supports the member states in protecting critical infrastructure against the risks, including terrorist risks, that we face. even though the responsibility for this type of infrastructure lies with the member states and the owners/operators who are generally related to them, it makes sense to make certain aspects of prevention, identification, classification of critical infrastructures and the assessment of the need to improve their protection community-wide. the development of the internet and the liberalisation of certain markets (electricity, gas, telecommunications, rail freight, etc.) must lead us to be very vigilant about our critical infrastructures, which are increasingly interconnected at european level and whose shutdown, whether permanent or temporary, or destruction could have serious repercussions for the health, safety, economic or social well-being of european citizens or for the proper functioning of the governments of the member states.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my spanish colleague alejo vidal-quadras on the prospects for the internal gas and electricity market, which provided an update on this matter after a long process of liberalising energy markets and, above all, the adoption by the european council in march 2006 of an energy package aimed at ensuring security of supply, competitiveness and environmental sustainability in the field of the european union's energy policy. i regret that the amendment tabled by my colleagues reul, laperrouze, trautmann and others, which i voted for, was not retained by parliament because it allowed a balanced and alternative path to the mere separation of network ownership while guaranteeing the independence of this separation. these are topics on which the political debate is far from over. the same applies to the role of regulators, the removal of barriers to interconnections, the development of new mass production from renewable energies, the considerable investments in infrastructure to meet growing needs, etc.
in writing. i voted against the vidal-quadras report on the prospects for the gas and electricity markets, which prepares in particular the presentation by the commission of a third 'liberalisation' package next september. firstly, i am opposed to the dogmatic liberal principle of ownership separation (ownership and management of the grid), as it provides no guarantees in terms of investment, supply, security or access of third parties and renewables to the grid. it also fails to ensure the availability of energy at the best price for citizens and does not fulfil public service obligations. why then upset the current organisation, which is working well and ensures the effective independence of the network managers, thanks in particular to a strong intervention by the regulator and the introduction of strict rules guaranteeing equal treatment and a quality service to all network users, even those living in regions with natural handicaps and the outermost regions. moreover, i believe that the problem of the independence of the transmission system operator is not a question of ownership but of regulation. why then ask for the energy operators to be de-publicised?
in writing. i regret the adoption of the separation of property by property advocated by the staunch defenders of the dismantling of large enterprises. i think that the liberal right has just dealt a new blow to the principle of public service, which is so dear to the european citizens. i consider that the asset separation does not provide any guarantees in terms of investment, security or third party access to the network (including renewable energy, which may be penalized by their high costs). nor does it ensure the availability of energy at the best price for citizens. i think it would have been preferable to maintain a french-style system, which incorporates into its operation the legislative rules derived from the previous european directives.
in writing. the ump delegation would like to recall and emphasise that asset separation is not the best response to the current market dysfunctions. in a context of strong competition, with the emergence of powerful non-european operators, it seems to us dangerous to dismantle european energy companies in the name of a dogmatic approach to competition policy, far removed from the industrial logic that should strengthen the european union in world competition. the european energy supply is a long-term strategic issue which requires ensuring its security beyond the duration of a single contract. this security of energy supply depends on investments which are already clearly insufficient. however, these will have to increase considerably to meet our future needs, whether for gas or electricity. the asset separation means that our traditional energy operators will not be able to make these investments in the energy networks. it is very dangerous and very worrying to hand this over to new entrants, who may not have the necessary financial means, or to non-european companies, who may not necessarily share our assessment of our future needs. in these circumstances, the ump delegation expects the european commission to develop an alternative approach to the division of assets.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is time for the union to take up this debate and we can welcome the green paper initiative. however, i fear that this initiative is not necessarily good news for european workers. the green paper is open to criticism both in terms of the method it uses and in terms of the guidelines it proposes. firstly, as regards the method: i regret that this consultation does not respect the procedure laid down in article 138 of the treaty, which gives the social partners a special status in matters of social policy. this derogation from the procedure is also denounced by the european trade union confederation. secondly, on the substance: a green paper must be impartial. he must ask questions without giving a priori answers. the european commission is making statements which are clearly ideological. this is the case when the traditional model is seen as an obstacle to employment. this is also the case when it declares that protection against dismissal is an obstacle to the dynamism of enterprises and lists workplace insecurity as a guarantee of modernity. there are fundamental principles and rights in europe and in international law as laid down by the ilo which must be respected. the contract for an indefinite period must be confirmed as the rule. the employee must be protected by legislation or collective bargaining or both. i would like to stress that collective bargaining must therefore remain the main source of labour law. finally, a word on the concept of flexicurity, which is based on principle. as defined here, it introduces a major imbalance in the distribution of competences between the union and the member states. the european union would impose flexibility and leave the responsibility for ensuring the safety of workers to the member states alone. our fellow citizens want a europe which protects their rights and their social model. we must not give them the impression that europe is destroying their social achievements. the challenge is their adherence to the european project, let us not forget that.
in writing. globalisation, ageing populations, and the acceleration of trade: these are all challenges that will be faced even more in the future than today. no member state can claim to achieve this alone, and it is through coordinated action with the european union that employment and social policy will be successful. i therefore welcome the own-initiative report on the modernisation of labour law, which is necessary to meet the challenges of the 21st century. its objective is not only commendable, it is vital. work must be given a new value, its legislative framework adapted to the times, and it will be necessary to enable those who want to work to work, by promoting attractive training, and those who want to work more power, by offering more flexibility to employee-employer negotiations. flexibility does not mean the end of protective rules, it means that these rules will be determined by free negotiation adapted to the needs of all, needs which will be expressed in a fostered social dialogue. france has already initiated this dialogue with the social partners, and i therefore welcome this report, which is in line with the ambitions and actions undertaken in france.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, as we take stock of the first railway package, it is clear that we are still far from the mark. despite the progress made, and in particular the fact that a decline which seemed inevitable has been halted, the modal share of rail is still too low. this is all the more regrettable in these times of climate change, when the choice of rail is confirmed every day by the news. the reasons for this half-hearted assessment are well known: too much emphasis has been placed on openness, the benefits of which must not be denied, without paying enough attention to the technical obstacles, in particular the lack of interoperability, knowing that it should have accompanied openness as it progressed, rather than following it in the distance. this is probably because liberalization generally costs the states little, while harmonization is another matter. today, at a time when the problems of interoperability are finally being tackled again, i am concerned that, under the guise of convenience, the objectives of transferring modes to rail in particular are being pushed into the background. instead of downward revision of the objectives, the intellectual and financial resources should have been revised upwards. i hope that this report will help to remind us of the way we still have to go to give rail back the place it deserves.

in writing. the new postal directive, which i voted against, is a case study in the commission's ideological obstinacy. by removing the reserved area on folds of less than 50g, the death sentence of the postal public service is signed. the commission and some members of this parliament are trying to make us believe that the 'universal postal service' is guaranteed by this directive. by rejecting the reserved area as a means of financing, we are faced with an impossible equation: the states - already limited in their budget - should finance the universal service. there is no economic or rational reason to exclude the 'reserved domain' from possible financing methods, except to call into question the universal postal service. precariousness, reduction in the number of post offices, increase in rates for private individuals, end of the equalization of rates and therefore equal access to the postal service... this is what has just been voted. i remain convinced that public services can operate as a network at european level. this is possible and desirable if we want to create a genuine european community. this directive makes us renounce the very function of politics: to regulate and control economic activity, the market, in order to achieve objectives of spatial planning, solidarity, development...
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my german colleague markus ferber on the completion of the internal market for postal services. firstly, i am pleased that the process of gradually and controlled opening up of the postal market, while ensuring the provision of universal service on a lasting basis, is continuing in accordance with the european council resolution of 1994. the political compromise reached between the european people's party (epp), the european socialist party (esp) and the liberal party (eldr) is good and balanced. the date proposed by the european parliament of 31 december 2010 is more realistic than the date proposed by the european commission of 1 january 2009. i voted for various amendments, in particular on the financing of the universal service which must be guaranteed at all times in a fully liberalised postal market and on the definition of this universal service which must guarantee collection and distribution at the home or premises of any natural or legal person every working day, including in isolated or sparsely populated areas. in addition, member states should ensure that a sufficient number of access points are established in rural and sparsely populated areas.
in writing. i voted against the draft postal directive because i am not satisfied with the amendments made by parliament to the commission's proposal for full liberalisation of the postal sector by 1 january 2009, in particular the postponement of two years. paradoxically, this new stage of liberalisation will lead to additional public expenditure, since the commission is at the same time requiring member states to choose a means of financing universal service obligations. the three financing options proposed have already been tried in some member states and have led to major litigation. in addition, the maintenance of the reserved domain (or residual monopoly on mail under 50 grams) was not retained, although it is one of the most efficient and transparent funding routes. the commission's proposal is to keep the area reserved for the european parliament, a policy which i support but which the commission and, today, the majority of members of the european parliament reject. i do not think that the commission's objectives of improving service - quality, price and choice - and unlocking the sector's growth potential can be achieved in this way. on the contrary, i fear the worst for the future of rural, mountainous and island areas.
in writing. i voted against the liberalization of postal services. i also supported the request to reject this directive on the grounds that the reasons for this proposal are contradictory and unrealistic as regards the guarantee of the universality of the service for which the means of financing do not safeguard the right to daily collection and dispatch of mail for all european citizens. finally, i consider that the setting of an a priori expiry date for directive 97/67 is not in line with the results of the consultation of the social partners concerned and of the member states, which have indicated the need to maintain the guarantees of universal service in a uniform, proportionate and equitable manner. in my view, this proposal offers no guarantee that the social aspects of this liberalization will be seriously addressed in order to avoid competition on the labour market and social dumping.
in writing. mr ferber's report on the liberalization of the postal sector does not solve any of the problems raised by the commission's text: the financing of universal service missions, and in particular those not mentioned in the directive and which exist in france in particular, such as the distribution of the press at a lower price, land planning, distribution 6 days a week, the bank for all ...; the implicit challenge of the single tariff and the tariff equalization by the obligation to reflect costs; the participation (concrete or financial) of private operators in public service obligations ... the text was based on a flawed study, which was wrong on some points and which ignored the real results of 10 years of partial liberalization of postal services. it could only be a bad text and a lame compromise. it is a source of legal insecurity and a social threat. the commission's real objective is now clearly apparent. as is usual in this type of case, the aim is not so much to make the services provided to the public and the community more efficient and cheaper as to break up public monopolies and allow private operators, preferably multinational ones, to screen out profitable markets.
in writing. the french post office is not a company like any other, it is a state-owned company, run by revolutionary trade unionists. it's a public service totally at the mercy of private corporate interests. why should we try to defend the public service of the post office when in reality it is not one? the client has no say and the unions claim to act in his best interests. the employer (the state) or the shareholders (every frenchman) are terrified to see the system blocked by certain employees represented by omnipotent and totalitarian unions. there is no counter-power to balance the rights and powers these employees have granted themselves, and it is the public interest that is being flouted. should the post office be liberalized? should we challenge this totally gangrenous system which does not seek to satisfy the customer, but only to sneak around, demonstrate and demand the maintenance of so-called "acquired" advantages? the answer is a resounding yes, and quickly. the postal service now has to make enormous efforts to overcome its major handicaps, which are: the huge wage bill, the weight of pensions and a complex, burdensome, costly and inefficient organisation.
in writing. i cannot accept this total deregulation and the abolition of the 'reserved domain' of the states for postal missions. this general opening to competition is undermining the single stamp tariff, equal treatment of territories and the presence of the postal service in disadvantaged sectors. even in the united states, there is no competition for ordinary mail - less than 50g - and its distribution is ensured by a federal agency. it is clear that the compensation mechanisms for universal service, reduced to a minimum, will in no way guarantee the public service and the extension of the deadline for the implementation of this liberalisation does not resolve anything in the matter. the european council of ministers has just decided to draw up a 'protocol on public services based on the treaty'. it would be right to suspend any new opening to competition in these services.
in writing. the commission's proposal aims to fully open up the eu postal services markets to competition by 2009, in line with the deadline set in the current postal directive. in this context, the european commission has proposed a text which aims to guarantee the financing of universal service by ending the 'reserved domain' and replacing it with new financing instruments. i am opposed to the total liberalization of postal services. the postal service is a public service which we must safeguard. that is why i co- tabled and voted for an amendment calling for the reintroduction of the 'reserved domain' as one of the means of financing the universal service. at present, there is no economic reason to abandon the reserved domain. this financing method, which is currently working very well, should be one of the options available to member states. since this option was not adopted by the european parliament's plenary, i voted against the final text to show my opposition to this unjustified liberalization.
in writing. by eliminating the reserved area which allowed the financing of the universal service, guaranteeing a quality public service for all, by disarming it by means of financing methods left to the choice of each member state, the total liberalization of postal services will result in the disappearance of solidarity between urban and rural areas, the enrichment of shareholders and the increase in the public deficit of local authorities. i therefore voted in favour of the amendment to reinstate the reserved area, which satisfies more than 70% of european citizens. i am a socialist and i am in favour of a postal europe with modern public services, but not at the cost of job losses and human and territorial solidarity. the paradox of this proposal is that, without a new directive, liberalisation will take effect on 1 january 2009. an amendment rejecting the text proposed by the gue makes this liberalisation effective from 1 january 2009, because at that time the 2002 directive applies, and only the 2002 directive applies, which is why i did not support this amendment. i voted in favour of the amendment rejecting the text, which also removed the date of 1 january 2009. i voted against the final text, of course.
in writing. i voted in favour of the compromise drafted by markus ferber because it improves on certain points the original proposal of the european commission. it gives the european posts additional time to prepare for opening up to competition, which has been postponed to 1 january 2011 instead of 2009 as originally planned by the commission. i also supported the compromise because it will protect the terms and conditions of employment of postal workers. the liberalization of markets cannot be at the expense of the workers, even if it is to the benefit of the consumers. our vote also provides security in terms of territorial cohesion. all users are guaranteed access to mail collection and distribution throughout the european union at least five days a week. however, there is still a major difficulty which will be the subject of the second reading. i want to talk about the financing of universal service. we need to have funding mechanisms that are legally secure and sustainable. this is a prerequisite for economic operators in the sector, without which i cannot commit myself to full liberalisation of the sector.
in writing. this report is important because it modernises the law of the single market in air transport, in particular with a view to ensuring the uniform application of community law in all member states and to creating a level playing field for all airlines. i am particularly pleased that amendments nos 35 and 61, for which i voted, were adopted by a large majority. the first calls for clarification of the provisions concerning the law applicable to workers employed in a country other than that of the airline employing them. the second calls on the commission to present clear legislation in this area. it seems to me important that in the present context, when air transport is constantly developing and when airlines are opening establishments in different countries of the union, the law applicable to workers in these establishments should be clearly established.

author. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the reason we have asked the council and the commission today is that the consent we are being asked to give to amend the trips agreement in order to make the transitional solution of august 2003 final raises many questions. following the debate in the parliamentary committee on this mechanism, all the experts interviewed were unanimous in their criticism of this solution, which only partially addresses the problems faced by countries lacking pharmaceutical production capacity and, therefore, the difficulties of access to care for their population. while it was supposed to provide a quick and effective response, this mechanism is considered complex and even inefficient. despite the commitment of the council and the commission to the parliament, no evaluation was carried out. so there are still doubts about him. "it has never been evaluated because it has never been used", the commission replies, claiming that this does not presuppose its ineffectiveness. that is a fine rhetoric in reverse logic, but it is by no means an argumentative response. the questions that parliamentarians are asking are: why has this solution never been used? does it respond to the scale of the problem? if not, what new actions should the union take to achieve the stated objective? there can be no discrepancy between the intentions expressed and the deeds. in its statements, the union supports the doha declaration, the trips flexibilities and the states which make use of them. it also undertakes not to require developing countries to apply new intellectual property rules that are more stringent than those provided for in the wto, as this would undermine effective access to treatment. yet these statements are not followed by effects. let's start by understanding each other. for example, what is meant by flexibility? for us, this concept encompasses all flexibilities, not just the 2003 solution. in its statements, the commission refers only to the latter. as for the intellectual property rules that go beyond the trips agreement, how do we define them? do we identify the same? in its statements, the commission refrains from resorting to such rules, but the negotiations carried out do not necessarily reflect this commitment. its representatives sometimes even justify the use of these in the name of the fight against counterfeiting, which is a completely different debate. finally, there must be clear political support for each country that uses any flexibility, which is not the case in practice. what we are asking for is transparency and a balance between public discourse and negotiations behind closed doors. we believe that the problem is much more than simply expressing agreement to an international protocol. this is a political and humanitarian problem of great magnitude which requires a genuine political will to rise to the challenge. we now want clear commitments on many points, all of which will be included in our resolution which will be voted on tomorrow. this requires a joint political declaration with parliament before we vote. we will not settle for another debate without a specific commitment. we want a solemn commitment from the council and the commission to ensure that europe is actively involved in finding new solutions and that it has the ambition to be, as our citizens want, a leading player in the fight for access to affordable medicines for everyone in the world.

the agenda calls for the report by lidia joanna geringer de oedenberg, on behalf of the committee on regional development, on the role and effectiveness of cohesion policy in reducing disparities in the poorest regions of the eu (2006/2176 (ini)) (a6-0241/2007).
member of the commission. madam president, it is a pleasure to come before parliament to exchange views on the geringer de oedenberg report on the role and effectiveness of cohesion policy in reducing disparities in the poorest regions of the european union. once again, as in the case of other own-initiative reports adopted by the committee on regional development, this proves the excellent collaboration between our two institutions. i am speaking on behalf of mrs hübner, who has had to go to romania, and she sends you her best wishes. i welcome this report and i appreciate its positive contribution to the debate on the impact and effectiveness of cohesion policy at a critical moment of the 2007-2013 programming period and on the eve of the budgetary review to be carried out in the year 2008/09. i fully share the view that the cohesion policy is not only essential but also effective in reducing socioeconomic and territorial disparities and in tapping the development potential of all eu regions. the value added of cohesion policy has already been proved, and we all recognise that it goes well beyond financial transfers to include, among other things, the development of partnerships, exchanges of best practice, budgetary stability and a strategic approach. i particularly appreciate the theme and the content of your report because it touches on the backbone of cohesion policy. indeed, the main goal of our policy is to reduce the socioeconomic and territorial disparities in the poorest eu regions. the challenge is not negligible. these disparities have dramatically increased following the recent enlargements, and cohesion policy is the only community instrument specially designed to this aim. for instance, disparities in gdp per head between the top and bottom 10% eu regions have almost doubled after the two most recent enlargements. in fact, regional disparities in the eu are very important, much more than within the united states or japan, or of a similar dimension to that in china and india for instance. despite impressive growth rates in the new member states and the convergence of many regions of the eu-15, there are still 70 regions – home to 123 million europeans – with a gdp per head below 75% of the eu average. in addition, there are a number of regions – the majority of which are among the most developed ones – which are losing ground. in 27 regions, gdp per head declined in real terms between the years 2000 and 2004 and, in another 24, growth was under 0.5% per year. nevertheless, as explained in full in the recently published fourth cohesion report, convergence is taking place. this is due both to the accelerated growth of most of the new member states and to the sometimes sluggish performance of some of the most advanced ones. on the whole, the periphery of the eu is catching up with the core of europe not only in terms of gdp per head but also of employment, productivity and other indicators, and this is good news. this includes the former cohesion countries which, with the exception of portugal, in the last few years have experienced impressive progress. this phenomenon – the long-term convergence process – is especially occurring at eu level between member states and regions. we know that, at national level, the picture is somehow different, since in many cases growth is increasingly concentrated in the capital region or in the main metropolitan areas, which deepens the internal disparities and causes problems related to agglomeration, like transport congestion, pollution, housing price rises and so on. let me underline the substantial contribution of our policy to this overall positive convergence process. independent evaluation studies have shown that cohesion policy has supported much-needed investment in infrastructure, human resources, modernisation and diversification of regional economies. between 2000 and 2005, public investment in the four cohesion countries has been around 25% higher than it would have been without cohesion policy. it has contributed to the growth of gdp. increasing gdp levels attributable to regional policy ranged from 10% in greece and 8.5% in portugal in the period 1989-1999, and 6% for greece and portugal, 4% in the german länder and 2.4% in spain in the period 2000-2006. preliminary estimates for 2007-2013 suggest an impact of between 5% and 9% in the new member states. it has also contributed to reduced social exclusion and poverty. cohesion policy cofinances the training of nine million people annually. more than half of them are women, leading to better employment conditions and higher income. for example, over 450 000 gross jobs were generated in six countries: denmark, france, the netherlands, spain, sweden and the uk. between 2000 and 2005 it accounted for two thirds of objective 2 funding. it has helped shift the policy mix of public investment in member states towards growth-enhancing investment. according to the most recent data, the amount of cohesion investment earmarked for research and development, innovation and information and communication technologies (icts) for 2007-2013 has more than doubled in comparison with the years 2000-2006. clearly, it remains to be seen how these plans will be implemented, but we already see, among both the member states and the regions, an increasing awareness in their development strategies for the next financial period. certainly, one of the keys of this success lies in the fact that cohesion policy is an integrated, fully-fledged policy; it is not a sectoral policy, or a disjointed bundle of sectoral policies, but an integrated instrument aimed at delivering specific tailor-made solutions for each european region or territory. at the same time, it is not just an eu policy that operates in isolation but it certainly depends on the active involvement of partners at national, regional and local level. your report correctly points to a number of issues which are particularly relevant for the poorest regions if they are to make the best use of the allocated funds. i shall mention just a few likely to provide them with appropriate technical assistance. the importance of designing tailor-made development strategies, or the value of implementing effective partnership and encouraging good practices. i took note of your proposals. i am convinced that some of them will find their way into the current legislative framework that has given rise to the new initiatives recently adopted by the commission, like the three ‘j’s – jasper, jeremy and jessica – or regions for economic change. the flexibility of cohesion policy makes it possible to implement the best measures adopted for each case. in this regard, mrs hübner will ensure that the commission pays particular attention to the needs of the poorest regions in the ongoing negotiations on the programming documents for the years 2007-2013. i also appreciate the contribution of your report to the debate on future cohesion policy, which was launched by the publication of the fourth cohesion report. i welcome these valuable recommendations aiming at increasing the efficiency of cohesion policy. as you know, we are now at the initial stage of reflection on the future of cohesion policy. this debate aims at nurturing the review of the eu budget that the commission has to undertake in the years 2008 and 2009. in conclusion, you are aware that the public consultation on the future of cohesion policy will be launched following the cohesion forum to be held at the end of september. a dedicated internet site will collect the contributions of member states, regions, cities, eu institutions, economic and social partners and, of course, civil society organisations. the commission intends to present the results of this consultation in spring 2008, together with the fifth progress report on economic and social cohesion. on the basis of this and other own-initiative reports recently approved, i am very much looking forward to parliament’s contribution to this debate.
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, like my colleague, mrs krehl, i congratulate you on your election and on your first presidency. commissioner potočnik, i would like to say that this report, which has been presented in an excellent way by our colleague, mrs geringer de oedenberg, is first of all a cry from the heart. it is also a necessity for the european union, as our colleague mr krehl has just said, and it is an appeal to the commission. it is a cry from the heart because the development of poor regions is not just the development of regions, it is the taking into account of situations, sometimes dramatic, of people who are unemployed, or who have to move, etc. so it's a cry from the heart on a human level. it is also a necessity - the report explains it well - for the development of the european union. having said that, commissioner, we must go further and not see my remarks as criticism but as a statement of fact. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. well, in our colleague's report there are a number of proposals. what i would like to say in the few seconds i have is that we need the commission to be clear today on the following level: who is doing what, when and how? the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this is an own-initiative report which was suggested by our political group and which, after several months of work, was supported by a very large majority of the committee on the internal market. i can only welcome this very broad support, because if our plenary confirms it, then we will have the opportunity, commissioner, to participate fully, to influence fully the work that the commission is doing to draw up, next autumn, a communication on the internal market strategy for the 21st century. the internal market is the european union's greatest achievement in more than 50 years. it is at the heart of the european project, and now of the lisbon strategy. however, this is a process which is constantly progressing and, above all, it is necessary to adopt a political approach to it - and i think this is the main originality of the report i am presenting to you. in these turbulent times in europe, it is important to understand that the deepening of the internal market will not be possible if it continues to face scepticism and even hostility from a large part of european public opinion, which often considers the internal market and competition policy to be the source of many of the social difficulties faced by our citizens. the aim of any internal market strategy must therefore be to transform this disbelief and hostility into confidence in the internal market, on the one hand, by showing the benefits of the internal market and, on the other hand, by pursuing at the same time the objectives of openness and competition and the objective of social cohesion with its various components: environment, employment, culture, access for vulnerable people. our report has tried to find that balance and i think that the reason why it has received such widespread support is that it has largely succeeded in doing so. this is the main recommendation we wish to make to the european commission: it is impossible to deepen and develop the internal market if our citizens do not support this policy. we have therefore proposed three lines: restoring confidence, reducing burdens and, finally, placing our internal market policy in the international context. that is why we have emphasized everything that has to do with the quality of life of our fellow citizens: the environmental dimension, consumer protection. we have asked for the national parliaments to be more closely involved in our work on this point, to understand better the importance of the internal market. an important amendment which i have put forward and which i think we will have general agreement on is amendment no 12 as amended. with this amendment, on the basis of the decisions of the european council of 21 june on the mandate given to the intergovernmental conference to insert a paragraph on public services in the new amending treaty, we call on the commission to clarify the situation of public services, gis and sgeis because we believe that in a successful internal market, supported by our citizens, the place of these services is very important. we have already seen this when we discussed the directive on the internal market in services. we have also placed a great deal of emphasis on smes and on the vulnerable, particularly the disabled. as regards the development of the right to consume, we find that there is very little crossborder consumption, about 6%, which is of course insufficient. we naturally include energy policy and the fight against global warming in the internal market, as does the opening up of network industries. one of the major - and controversial - proposals is to include an internal market test in any new legislation. that's just what i wanted to say in a nutshell. if we succeed in combining the intrinsic strength of the internal market with the commitment of producers and consumers to this policy, then i believe that this will be a real lever for prosperity, for employment and for the preservation of the european social model at the same time as the economic strength of europe as a player on the world stage.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: mr president, commissioner, it is my duty to present the position of the economic and monetary committee and, for once, if i may say so, with pleasure, the rapporteur whom we had appointed has refused to present this report on his own behalf, because he regretted that the vote of the economic and monetary committee had led to insistence on the fiscal conditions of a harmonious internal market. in short, your committee on economic and monetary affairs considers that for the internal market to function harmoniously, certain initiatives must come from the commission to combat distortions in terms of taxation. i can only support the view of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. there are two other points which i think are important to stress today. the first is the operation of competition policy. recent events have shown us again, if need be, particularly in the field of credit rating agencies, that a single market requires a rigorous competition policy which applies to all market sectors. the other dimension - and the rapporteur has mentioned it - is the international dimension and the capacity of the european union, in the functioning of its internal market, to make it a driving force for standardization at international level. this is even more true today in the area of financial markets and i hope that here too the commission will take the initiative in proposing, at international level, the standardisation we need to make progress in terms of supervision.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the competitiveness of enterprises and the efficiency of the internal market also require appropriate and modern legal statutes for enterprises. a step forward for large companies was taken with the adoption of the regulation on the statute for a european company on 8 october 2001. in 2004, the european commission launched a reflection on a new form of european company, more specifically designed for small and medium-sized enterprises: the european private company. this initiative was very much appreciated by all those who had been waiting for it for thirty years, i say thirty years. the results of the commission's feasibility study on this status were presented in december 2005. it is clear that the vast majority of economic operators interviewed are in favour of such a status for two main reasons: firstly, the introduction of a european status would have the advantage of removing obstacles to the establishment and mobility of smes within the european union. it would also make it possible to create a european label for smes, especially those in the countries which have recently joined the european union. the european private company appears to smes as an effective tool for entering the european market. its adoption would also be an indirect factor in the development and harmonization of national laws, which in turn would promote the development and integration of the european economy. this new statute would respond to the need to simplify and make more effective the legal tools available to businesses. i am convinced that many small and mediumsized enterprises would benefit from such a status, which would of course remain optional. this project of a european private company is strongly supported by the economic circles of almost all the member states. this is of course the case in france and germany. parliament has approved mr lehne's own-initiative report, and i support the conclusions. but right now, nothing is moving. that is why i support the questions to the european commission put by my colleague, mr gargani, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs. it is important to know what the underlying problems are which are causing the commission to delay its work in this area.

i think it is indisputable that conditions should be attached to the granting of subsidies. but the fact that these conditions are always subject to heavy sacrifices for the employees is the problem. in this respect, if mood has rarely been the primary characteristic of the successive commissioners i have known, if social fibre is clearly not part of their attributes, this time the commission's flagship directorate-general has done even more by demonstrating that political issues leave it as indifferent as social problems. by threatening the very existence of this emblematic place in poland, is the commission measuring the political significance of the message it is thus sending to the people of this new member country, barely three years after its accession? the agenda calls for the oral question to the commission on the creation of functional airspace blocks for the establishment of the single european sky (com (2007) 0101 final) by paolo costa, on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism (o-0035/2007 - b6-0135/2007).
author. mr president, first of all we must give back to caesar what is his, or to another italian, namely paolo costa, who is in fact the true author of this written question and who asked me to be kind enough to take his place in his absence and to put it before you. this is an oral question with debate to the commission on the state of play of the creation of functional airspace blocks for the establishment of the single european sky, in other words, on the commission's intentions with regard to the implementation, or the state of progress in the implementation as it can be seen today, of the package of texts which had resulted in a conciliation in december 2003 and which was called the 'single sky package'. one of these texts provided for the rearrangement of functional space blocks, i.e. the routes of airliners to the different floors of airspace, in order to optimise consumption, reduce greenhouse gases and, if possible, reduce congestion at the busiest airports, not to mention the possibility of reducing the cost of air transport. the issue is particularly sensitive, with reluctance on the part of the member states, which have always reaffirmed their sovereignty over their airspace. this is particularly the case in the member states - and i know one of them, the one i come from, is very dear to me - which have a large military force and military space blocks reserved almost at their discretion. the concern of paolo costa is that this text - one of the four on the single sky - on the rearrangement of space blocks has apparently not advanced as feared, and that it has been the subject of very strong resistance from the member states. the question that mr paolo costa is asking the commission is therefore as follows. a communication has just been produced by the commission which clearly acknowledges that the cost of the absence of functional airspace blocks for the establishment of the single european sky is about eur 1 billion. the first question is whether the commission can accept this and whether it considers that the implementation of regulation (ec) no 551/2004 on the organisation of the airspace is proceeding satisfactorily. how does the commission explain the fact that no new functional airspace blocks have become operational since the entry into force of this regulation? article 10 of this regulation provides for the extension of airspace organisation to lower airspace and asks the commission to provide for any other appropriate measures 'in the light of progress made'. on this basis, what changes does the commission consider appropriate to the current legislation? finally, would the commission agree not to wait until the end of 2008 to propose a proposal to this effect? last question by paolo costa there are several questions in one: does the commission agree with the failure of the bottom-up approach which left it to the member states to create functional airspace blocks among themselves and does it not think that it is now necessary to adopt a more proactive approach on the part of the european union? i believe that this is the question that mr costa is asking the european commission, without betraying the spirit of the question.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to congratulate mrs jeggle on her excellent work. i support in particular his opposition to the abolition of aid for private storage of cream and skimmed milk powder and his desire to introduce a single rate of aid for milk distributed in schools. i would like to mention, however, as some of my colleagues have done, the current shortage of milk, which is due to an increase in world demand but also to a decline in supply which could have been anticipated because, in my opinion, it was foreseeable. as a result of the cap reform and the lower price paid to milk producers, some farmers, as in france, have disposed of part of their dairy cows in favour of beef or, as in germany, have completely abandoned beef for cereals. france is short of 100 000 dairy cows to meet its quota and the european union would need 1 000 million litres of milk to meet european demand. this shortage has already had and will have a significant impact on the prices of milk and, therefore, milk products, as well as on the prices of many other food products. these increases will be in addition to the price increases for other basic foodstuffs such as cereals or meat due to the increase in feed prices. all this will of course create additional difficulties for consumers. i therefore believe that it is necessary to put in place price stabilization instruments. this would include, as soon as possible, the replenishment of new stocks to secure the market; increase the price of milk paid to producers to encourage them to maintain and increase their production and to help them cope with the increase in feed prices; to better regulate marketing and distribution channels; to increase european milk production quotas as quickly as possible; to assess the milk cmo during the cap health check in 2008, in the light of the current shortage and before considering any abolition of milk quotas in 2015. i would like to conclude by mentioning the even more difficult situation of the milk producers in the mountain areas, the producers whom i represent, whose production costs are higher and whose supply is more difficult. moreover, in some countries, such as france, they face a reduction in the collection aid which compensated for part of the extra cost of collecting in mountain areas. milk production is one of the sectors which best contributes to the maintenance of spaces and to land use planning, especially in difficult areas. i hope therefore that the specific features of mountain areas will be taken into account in future debates on the health check and the new cap.

in writing. once is not always enough: the commission's proposal to harmonise the rules for the transport of dangerous goods is a step in the right direction. the text proposed to us is intended to simplify and unify existing community legislation. at present, no less than four directives and numerous commission decisions govern the transport of dangerous goods by road, rail or inland waterway. this disparate set of rules makes them too complex, difficult to transpose into national legislation and often obsolete. the subject is particularly important because the volume of internal transport in the european union is constantly increasing. the number of dangerous goods is also increasing. almost 110 billion tonne-km/year of these goods are transported in the union each year, or 8% of all goods transported. france, with its strategic position at the crossroads of europe, regularly sees its road, rail and river networks congested and therefore particularly prone to transport accidents. it is high time that all the peripheral and superfluous european legislation on this subject was abolished in order to enable the various operators but also the national authorities to ensure and fully strengthen the safety of this type of transport.
