the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be able to present to you today this report on the allocation of macrofinancial assistance to lebanon. it is a testament to the european union's commitment to helping the country recover from the successive crises it has been through. lebanon is now one of the most indebted countries in the world, with a debt equivalent to 180% of its gdp. the impact of the civil war from 1975 to 1990, the conflict with israel in the summer of 2006, chronic political instability and economic policy erraticities have led to a severe economic, financial and social crisis in the country. the reality of this situation calls for urgent action. however, the funds linked to the adoption last january of the eu-lebanon action plan under the european neighbourhood policy will only be available from 2009. the exceptional macro-financial assistance we are about to adopt will close this gap and will have an immediate impact on lebanon's public finances and balance of payments, provided it is implemented without delay. this assistance will take the form of a donation of eur 30 million, supplemented by a loan of eur 50 million to help the lebanese state complete post-war reconstruction and continue its economic recovery. my report fully endorses the need for this financial aid to lebanon. it also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are respected. first of all, it should be noted that this aid must be strictly complementary to the funding provided by the bretton woods institutions, the paris club, bilateral donors and europe under other programmes. it must be consistent with the union's external policies or means of action already in place and ensure the added value of the community's engagement. it is also necessary that the council explicitly and publicly endorses the recommendations of parliament as regards the conditions and criteria for the granting of this assistance, namely the improvement of transparency and sustainability of public finances, the application of defined macroeconomic and budgetary priorities, the implementation of specific provisions to avoid the risks of fraud, corruption and misuse of funds, the distribution of assistance in a fair balance between post-conflict spending, reconstruction, excessive debt and the social needs of the population, and full compliance with international standards on democracy, respect for human rights and the fundamental principles of the rule of law. the disbursement of such assistance to lebanon should be conditional upon the achievement of real progress towards the above objectives, which should be contained in a memorandum of understanding agreed with the lebanese authorities. i would also like to mention, in addition to the substantive work we have done on this text, the difficulties encountered in the practical preparation of this report, given the urgency with which it was dealt with. in future, therefore, any decision on the granting of macrofinancial assistance would require the commission and the council to consult us much earlier. in order for parliament to do its job properly, it is essential that it be better informed in good time. in this respect, the establishment by the commission of an early warning system would ensure a faster handling of the case by the competent parliamentary committee and avoid unnecessary delays, which could have detrimental consequences for the final beneficiary. the quality and consistency of our work, and the quality of our collaboration with the other institutions, depend heavily on this. in continuity with parliament's previous resolutions, i would also stress that such an important instrument cannot be regarded as merely exceptional. it must be based on a normal legal basis and not just on an ad hoc council decision taken on a case-by-case basis. a framework regulation on macro-financial assistance established under co-decision is necessary to strengthen transparency, accountability, monitoring and reporting systems. we must therefore consider the possibility of starting an interinstitutional discussion on the appropriate legal basis for this type of instrument. in the case of macrofinancial assistance to lebanon, which is both a country covered by the european neighbourhood policy and classified as a developing country, it seems to us that the legal basis on which this act should have been based should have been article 179 instead of article 308 of the ec treaty. it is precisely because lebanon is a developing country that parliament also insists on not neglecting the social aspect of the reforms which the lebanese government would be called upon to undertake. according to the united nations development programme, nearly 24% of lebanese live in conditions of extreme poverty and 52% are considered disadvantaged. in addition, illiteracy affects nearly 9% of the population, less than a third of the population finishes primary school and only 13% of lebanese reach university level. despite this reality, it is clear that at present the social question is not at the centre of the lebanese political debate and that the social aspect of the planned reforms is very limited compared to the economic and financial aspect. it is in the interest of lebanon and its partners, as i have already stressed, to find a fair balance in spending, especially on education and training. it must be borne in mind that persistent social inequalities can have serious economic and political consequences, which can contribute to the instability of the country.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report which has been presented to you is relatively important on the eve of the bali conference. international trade is growing, as we know, at twice the rate of the world's gross domestic product. as it grows, it first leads to an increase in the transport sector, one of the most productive sectors of greenhouse gases. secondly, it allows for a relocation of productive activity, which may be optimal in terms of the implementation of productive forces and the use of wage rules, but which, insofar as it does not take into account the greenhouse gas costs that this division of labour generates, can in turn accelerate the production of greenhouse gases and climate change. to give you a single figure, the ship, which carries 40 times more cargo than the airplane, produces only twice as many greenhouse gases, but we still fly the goods to optimize the production cycle. so i think that after the stern report, after the four reports of the intergovernmental panel on climate change, we are aware that, after all, it is worth waiting half a day or even three days more for a commodity to arrive on its market, rather than destroying the climate at a cost that the stern report estimates at five trillion dollars. the report before you, beyond this observation, tries to open up some avenues. there are obviously all the transportation-related tracks. we welcome the recent vote on the integration of aviation into the european system of quotas. the report calls for a reflection on industrial organization reducing the geographical scale of production circuits - producing closer to the final consumer - and it makes a number of proposals on trade in environmental goods itself. we propose, both in the wto and in bilateral or bi-regional agreements - in short, all the agreements we are negotiating at the moment - to give priority to the assessment of the effects on climate change in the environmental impact assessments of these agreements, to the significant reduction of all tariff and non-tariff barriers - we are thinking in particular of royalties - which oppose trade in clean goods and services, those which save the production of greenhouse gases. all this must of course be done in the most multilateral possible framework, preferably in the wto, if not in the bi-regional agreements that europe is currently negotiating. but we cannot rule out the possibility that after 2012, in the first post-kyoto period, humanity has not yet reached a unanimous agreement on the fight against climate change. if so, it is certain that the choices europe makes to be a leader in the fight against climate change may harm some of its sectors. not all of them. in many cases, being a leader in the climate change sector means gaining a competitive edge. in some cases, and i am thinking particularly of cement, this can cause enormous problems and there is a risk of cement tourism. in that case, after all the possibilities for multilateral agreements have been exhausted, we propose that you adopt what is provided for in article 20 of gatt, namely border adjustment taxes which restore fair competition. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the essence of my proposals.

mr president, like all my colleagues, i voted for mrs roure's report on combating racism and xenophobia by means of criminal law. i did so because i agree with the guidelines, but also because the rapporteur and the committee on civil liberties have put forward a text which is concerned with protecting freedom of thought, research and expression. any such decision carries a risk: it gives a political authority the right to tell people what is lawful or unlawful to think, say or write. in my country, we have seen inappropriate laws: mr gollnisch wanted to include in school curricula flattering mentions of france's colonial work. more subtly, laws whose orientation was not in doubt, such as that of mrs taubira, were misinterpreted or abused to initiate unjustified legal actions against historical works whose objectivity, intellectual rigor and more generally scientific quality had been unanimously praised by the community of historians. the opinion we have voted seems to me to be of a nature to prevent such deviations. firstly, because freedom of expression is solemnly recognized as a fundamental right and secondly because the framework decision is not intended to punish observations, analyses or opinions, but, which is quite different, incitement to hatred. i hope that all the member states and all the political groups will show the same concern for balance and wisdom as our rapporteur.
in writing. after more than five years of negotiations, the council finally reached agreement on the framework decision on combating certain forms and manifestations of racism and xenophobia by means of criminal law. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. as mrs roure's report points out, the framework decision establishes only a minimum level of harmonisation. its effectiveness and scope are largely reduced by the many derogations it provides for. despite the efforts of the european parliament, consulted on this text, to give it more force, the framework decision remains a text that lacks ambition and is not up to the challenges at stake: the fight against racism and the sharing of our universal values. this framework decision must be seen as a first step towards a genuine fight against racism and xenophobia at european level and maximum harmonisation in this field. despite these imperfections, i supported the adoption of this report in plenary because it is essential that the european union, and the european parliament in particular, send a strong political message in favour of fundamental rights.
in writing. i agree with the minority opinion formally expressed by my colleague mr dillen. the framework directive on criminal sanctions against 'certain forms and manifestations of racism and xenophobia' is a liberticidal law at european level, as deadly for freedom of thought and expression as the gayssot or taubira laws in france. thus, no political discourse in defence of national identities, of national historical pride, of the fight against the flow of migration or the dangers posed to the freedom of each and every one by the islamization of our continent is no longer immune from the fury of the thought police. once again europe is playing against europeans, because in the minds of the drafters of this directive and in the minds of the members who have just voted for it, there is no doubt about the alleged criminals and the alleged victims. in terms of criminal harmonization, at a time when police officers are being shot at gunpoint in the french suburbs, when our continent is still threatened by murderous terrorist acts, when repeat offenders take advantage of the abolition of borders to perpetrate horrors in several countries, there is more urgent than the formalization of the intellectual and judicial dictatorship of foreign preference and forced multiculturalism.
in writing. the subject of mrs roure's report is the fight against racism. this is a very laudable objective, but unfortunately it is used as a pretext for the implementation of a discriminatory policy against the nationals of our countries, who become second-class citizens in their own countries. two tragic events last sunday illustrate this. the murder of a young french woman, anne-lorraine schmitt, by a turkish-born repeat rapist, did not make the headlines, unlike the deaths on the same day of two "young women", moushin and larami, who, driving at high speed and without helmets, crashed into a police car on an unlicensed mini-motorcycle. the tv news reports have been widely commented on this accident; the president of the republic received the parents of the two teenagers. so, to benefit from the compassion of the state, do we have to burn and sack a city like the hundreds of scoundrels who claimed to want to avenge the death of their "friends" moushin and larami? why are innocent victims entitled to less consideration than criminals? it is high time that the causes of these aberrations were put to an end: the laxity of the authorities, the insane immigration policy pursued for 30 years and a so-called anti-racism which in france is akin to a real anti-french racism.
in writing. the european union is not just a large market, it is above all a union of peoples who share the same values and in particular the protection of everyone's fundamental rights. it was therefore urgent that the framework decision on combating certain forms of racism and xenophobia by means of criminal law should finally be adopted. europe is actively fighting racism and discrimination. this is why an instrument guaranteeing the same protection in all member states against racist and xenophobic acts is necessary. we must ensure a fair balance by ensuring an equivalent level of punishment for words and actions inciting violence and hatred, while guaranteeing the right to free expression. we respect national traditions as to whether or not to condemn denialism. i regret, however, that the ambition of this proposal has been reduced by the rule of unanimity in the council. and i urge the member states to go further, together with the european parliament, when reviewing this text.
in writing. the text adopted today marks an important milestone for the audiovisual media sector but also for european citizens. it is the result of a long negotiation in which the european parliament has played a major role. it significantly improves on the original proposal of the european commission, in particular on the extension of the scope of the directive to new media and the promotion of european audiovisual works. these points ensure that traditional and digital audiovisual media can develop competitively while ensuring the cultural diversity that is europe's identity. the recognition of a right of access to short extracts is also a real step forward for broadcasters, including pan-european broadcasters, provided that this right is exercised under reasonable conditions. finally, for the first time, we will have clear rules on product placement. this practice, which already exists, is currently evolving outside any regulatory framework, to the detriment of transparency and legal certainty. with the guarantees we are offered, product placement will open up new opportunities for european audiovisual production and creation, while ensuring the necessary protection and information for consumers.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the directive which parliament is to adopt at second reading is extremely important because it is the first directive requiring member states to have an environmental strategy to restore the good ecological condition of the seas and oceans. we have already stressed its importance in the first reading of the report because recent scientific reports show that the survival of fisheries resources and biodiversity in the seas and oceans is particularly threatened. some even say that in fifty years there will be no fish left. in addition, the oceans play a fundamental regulatory role for the climate and their pollution risks reducing this regulatory function, accentuating the negative effects of climate change. it was therefore urgent and necessary for the european union, having adopted a framework directive on water, in particular fresh water, to tackle the question of marine waters quickly. we have already expressed our desire to improve the existing text. i would like to begin by recalling the structural aspects of this directive and the existing texts. the first was to restore the ecological balance of our seas and oceans. the second step was to define the necessary steps for each member state: first, to work together within the marine regions or subregions; the second is to define what the water and biodiversity status was in these seas. the commission has also proposed that the member states should set up a european environment agency, which would be responsible for the coordination of environmental policy. so we found this directive to be positive, but we found it to be insufficient as it came from the commission. we have emphasized several points. firstly, the requirement that this directive be binding. binding on means, binding on results. and this is perhaps the most positive aspect of our cooperation with the council and the commission: the directive is binding. secondly, we wanted the definition of good ecological status to be rigorous so that restoration of this good status is not a wishful thinking. we have been largely satisfied that the criteria for good ecological status include the pressure of all the pollution affecting an ecosystem and the need to assess and reduce its impact in order to restore this good ecological status. thirdly, parliament is very much in favour of the establishment of marine protected areas, which are a kind of reserve and which must play a vital role in restoring the diversity of the biotope and in particular in restoring fish stocks. we would have liked a more binding, more rigorous and more severe text on the need for these reserves, but the principle has been retained. in any case, the need for them to be of sufficient size to play this role of restoring biodiversity is retained. finally, parliament wanted the scope of the directive to be extended. we particularly wanted to ensure that coastal waters were taken into account, and we did not want to remain in the dark about the need to take into account all the waters affected by tides. in any case, for a large part of them this has been the case. we would have liked to have been a little more forceful in defining the tidal return, but the text is satisfactory. i would like to stress the importance of coherence in the strategies by geographical area: we would have liked a tougher text, but the need for coherence is affirmed. finally, our baltic colleagues wanted the baltic states to be a kind of pilot project which would allow us to move faster in view of the urgency of the situation. they could not be fully satisfied because the tradition in our courts is not to mention any particular sector. nevertheless, the idea of a pilot zone is retained and i have no doubt that the commission will retain the baltic within this framework. finally, the timetable: for us the main thing was that the directive should be binding, even if the time-limit given to the member states to achieve this was extended a little. this is the compromise that was finally agreed. the deadline is 2020, but member states must act quickly because they will have to transpose the directive by 2010. i would also ask them not to waste time, because the water directive is running behind schedule and our seas may not be able to wait.
for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we remember the who appeal launched on 5 october 2006 which challenged the international community to improve air quality. the aim was to adopt the strictest standards for air pollution and to reduce the number of deaths in polluted cities by 15%. the european union, which is often at the forefront of environmental regulation, was very disappointed at first reading, to the point that our environment commissioner, mr dimas, was personally outraged by the european parliament's position, which weakened existing legislation which was already not very voluntary. the green group had warned the environment committee at second reading on 9 october 2007 of the counterproductive effects of administrative simplification, namely the increase in the number of days allowed for exceeding the maximum values and the extension of the derogations covering certain pollutants. the compromise reached at the european parliament's second reading, which was negotiated recently, limits the damage in comparison with the first reading. for pm 2.5 in urban areas, a new concentration threshold of 20 micrograms per cubic metre is proposed, which should be reviewed by the european commission in 2015. of course, additional devices could be activated to take account of the situation of sensitive populations, such as children and the elderly. even if it improves the initial situation, this compromise is not a great step forward for our european parliament. it will not oblige member states to take the binding measures necessary to improve the health of the european population. the impact of air pollution is still estimated to be nine months less life expectancy for our citizens. so we must go further and integrate more upstream the limitation of particulate matter from prevention instruments aimed at limiting emissions from sectors, in particular transport, as well as those from industries.
mr president, we have all acknowledged, and we all say, that our towns and cities are becoming more and more polluted and that, unfortunately, the number of deaths caused by pollution is increasing. i myself, who presides over an air quality monitoring network in my department, having already set it up more than 16 years ago, would like to point out that reducing air pollution is perceived by our fellow citizens as the priority for action by the public authorities in the field of environmental protection, and that it is even the main concern of 54% of the french. this text thus provides a response to the increase in respiratory diseases such as asthma, bronchitis and emphysema, which primarily affect young children - let us not forget bronchiolitis in the youngest children during the winter - and lung cancers in the youngest. the introduction of new standards for the finest, most harmful particles, which were not regulated until now, is therefore a satisfactory measure. but we have a multitude of solutions for better air quality: actions on fuels, on modes of transport, on vehicles. the package of community legislation which we already have and which, unfortunately, is not respected in most member states, would still have to be applied. the texts we are voting on tomorrow require member states to set up collection points in urban areas. in fact, everyone should have "particle plans". we also need to provide the public, especially sensitive people, with daily information on particulate matter in ambient air. finally, we must not forget the quality of indoor air, where we sometimes spend more than 80% of our time. little attention is paid to studies of the quality of the indoor environment, whereas the health impact is certainly at least as important as that of the outdoor environment.

member of the commission. mr president, i agree that fire is a permanent threat to consumers’ lives. research estimates that the number of fatalities per million inhabitants per year is 10.8 in the uk, 6 in spain, 11.8 in france, 15.7 in sweden and 7.3 in germany. so, as commissioner for consumer protection, this is a matter of major concern for me. thank you for remembering this important issue. let me recall the tragic case involving a british family whose two children were killed by carbon monoxide poisoning in a hotel room in corfu in october 2006. i have received several letters from you about this case. we contacted the greek authorities and they informed us that the hotel where the accident happened had its licence immediately revoked and has not been operating since then. i know that legal proceedings are taking place in greece and i hope they will come to a clear conclusion very soon. this is an emblematic case, but unfortunately this is not the only one. fire safety in hotels has been at the centre of discussions with the member states for the last 20 years. first, the results that have been achieved so far. council recommendation 86/666/ec on fire safety in existing hotels has helped to improve safety levels, especially in those countries where no or scarce regulation was available. furthermore, the construction products directive sets up specific requirements in the event of an outbreak of fire for all construction works, including hotels. several measures have been adopted to ensure a consistent application of this directive in the member states, such as a common system for classifying fire resistance of construction products and a number of harmonised european standards in the fields of fire-fighting, alarm and alerting equipment. in addition, the requirements of the council recommendation addressing the risks linked to electrical lighting have been implemented by the low voltage directive. however, there is still a lot of ground to cover in making all hotels in europe equally safe, whether existing or new and regardless of their size and accommodation facilities. as we know, the requirements are for the hotels that have at least 20 rooms. in its various discussions with the member states, the commission has noted that no common way forward for an eu-wide action has yet been agreed upon and that the proper enforcement of national legislation is, so far, the main priority. this issue of compliance is indeed a problem that should not be underestimated, and i am really sad to say this. this is why i have asked the major hotel chains present in europe to come to brussels for a meeting with me on 8 february 2008. obviously, until we have this legislation in place, we should take our immediate action. we will discuss the hotel safety issue and i will report back to you on the results of this consultation. if we can do it together with parliament – if parliament would like to participate in this meeting on 8 february – i will be more than glad to have this meeting with you. the collection of eu-wide data and statistics is a critical point: absence of statistical definitions and homogeneity in the way fire accidents are registered in the member states makes comparability a very difficult and inaccurate exercise. i would like to move on to the point of standardisation. standardisation without the support of a legal framework, such as a european directive or even a revised recommendation, would severely reduce its impact, and the ultimate objective of ensuring fire safety in hotels would be frustrated as a result. coming to the issue of sprinklers: their efficiency in reducing the devastating effect of fires has been largely demonstrated, but the cost of their installation and maintenance is not always compatible with the type of hotels that are mostly present in europe, such as small, family-type hotels. next to this, the decision of whether sprinklers or any other fire-fighting device should be compulsory in hotels falls within the exclusive competence of the member states. i would be glad to discuss with the member states and to support such measures if they are ready to take such steps. parallel to these developments on the regulatory side, it should be mentioned that hotels are adopting self-regulating performance-based codes and design methods. i think that hotel chains such as accor should be really supported in their efforts. the commission is not only dealing with fire safety in hotels under its profile as a service, but is also targeting, in a comprehensive strategy against fire risk, all those products that are largely present in hotels and most likely to be either the source of a fire or its accelerant. the initiatives of rip cigarettes, on which the chair of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, ms mccarthy, gave us a very important contribution, flammability of upholstered furniture, and nightwear and child-resistant lighters are the pillars of such a strategy. i am looking forward to continuing our cooperation on this very important issue which is a major concern for all of us. i would like once more again to thank parliament and especially the president because we are taking concrete measures with what is in our hands right now.

rather difficult. it has set itself the objective of increasing its acceptance by all actors. it recommends that questions arising from the community framework be distinguished from those relating to national implementation. it stresses the importance of the principle of subsidiarity, the need to adapt standards and requirements to local risks and requirements, and the importance of a common framework guaranteeing equal treatment for european farmers. this double layer of rules has made the implementation of the system very difficult. information to farmers was not sufficient; the risk criteria were not used extensively; the management, control and reduction system is too complex; the accounting for minor non-compliances has not been adequate; the control rates are not harmonised; the prior notification of controls is problematic. i personally do not wish to call into question the spirit of conditionality, which meets the legitimate expectations of our society: respect for the environment, traceability, food safety, transparency. i would like to stress, however, the burdensome nature of the regulations, the difficulties of applying them on the ground and the negative perception of some farmers, who feel that their professionalism and know-how are being called into question. i therefore support the need for simplification. i was disappointed by the commission's proposals, which were very limited, but i hope that parliament's proposals will be taken up and that the commission will make more ambitious ones when it comes to the health check. i would like to receive agricultural aid. agricultural aid would in a way restore conditions of fair competition with farmers in third countries who are not subject to the same production conditions. i think that it is because farmers receive public aid that they have to respect certain production rules in return. the aim is to establish a genuine contract between farmers and the european union. we have to go from coercion to contract, sort of. i am therefore pleased that my amendment on this subject has been adopted and that the farmer is required, when making his single application and declaring the area used for agricultural purposes, to also commit to respecting criteria of public health, animal welfare and respect for the environment. the reductions in payments must be different depending on whether the infringement is intentional or merely due to negligence, and i have also insisted that the penalty be proportionate to the importance of the area concerned by the non-compliance on the farm, particularly where polyculture and livestock farming are combined. the same rules must also be binding on farmers in the different member states and it is therefore necessary to ensure a harmonious transposition of the regulatory management requirements contained in the directives. i also welcome the adjustment measures for the new member states. on the other hand, while i am in amendment no 16. if this were the case, most infringements leading to aid cuts would not be punished and the system of aid conditionality would no longer make sense. i therefore ask you to support mr mulder's amendment no 31, which proposes a threshold of 100 euro, a compromise which i think could be supported by all.

in writing. for once we were tempted to vote in favour of a report by this parliament on vat. the committee was in favour of abandoning the objective of a definitive system based on taxation in the country of consumption, which alone justified further harmonization of rates. it also favoured the application of the subsidiarity principle, which would allow member states to apply a reduced or zero rate of vat to services provided locally, such as catering or other areas, in order to meet social, educational, cultural and other objectives. it also provides for the maintenance until 2010, when the vat directive is to be reviewed, of many derogations which should have expired in 2007. all of this is fine with us. however, the desire to maintain european vat legislation and the desire to achieve identical rates at all costs in the name of simplifying trade and customs formalities in intra-european trade cannot satisfy us. taxation is a matter for the sovereign states and the disparities in one type of taxation often outweigh the inequalities in another. so they are not always illegitimate.
in writing. the commission has been wrong about vat time and again. in the 1980s the cockfield report called for a range of vat rates. in the end, there is only a 15% floor and 5% floor for the normal and reduced rates. then the european commission wanted vat at the rate of the country of origin. the practice has imposed vat at the rate of the country of destination. it was a temporary scheme, it is becoming definitive, the "bolkenstein vat" has not been passed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's budget is not used to the detriment of the community's own resources. the commission will at least provisionally give way on its list in annex h to the sixth directive of 1977. because she finds out that a german has little chance of taking his mercedes for a cross-border lunch at the low-vat restaurant. it is a pity that it did not realise in 1993 that without border controls, intra-community vat was an inexhaustible mine of massive fraud. the philosophical logic of vat, a smart tax because it is economically neutral, is inaccessible to most commission officials. that explains their incessant legislative failures for the last 20 years.
in writing. as rapporteur, i welcome the adoption of this report on the establishment of a joint undertaking for the innovative medicines initiative (imi). the establishment of this public/private partnership between the european federation of pharmaceutical industries (efpia) and the european commission is a key and promising step forward for large-scale research programmes. the european commission must look at the needs of europe from a different angle. limi will have a total budget of eur 2 billion for the period 2008-2013. the european commission's €1 billion contribution will be paid to smes and universities. in return, the large companies will match this amount by a contribution in kind. they will involve these same smes and universities by providing them with tools and methods to better predict the safety and efficacy of medicines, smart infrastructures and knowledge management. this cooperation will enable large companies, small research centres, smes and universities to put their research projects into practice. the imi will thus contribute to improving knowledge transfer within universities and enterprises, and to the involvement of small enterprises in european research.

for the greens/efa group mr president, i would like to welcome the interest of the annual report before us. this is a substantial body of work which gives us an exhaustive overview of the initiatives taken during a year, under two presidencies, to implement the union's human rights policy. of course, it is not a trivial matter. it is a practical tool and a reference document. however, i think mrs andrikienė is right, this report lacks a sense of perspective, analysis and critical thinking, and as a result, it does not draw conclusions from the facts it sets out, and therefore it lacks recommendations. the failures or successes of this policy are not sufficiently highlighted. i hope and i am sure that this will be the work of the members in the report which parliament will draw up in the spring. they will have to move in this direction. there are also some awkward silences in this report. the chapter 'ms ludford spoke about it' which is devoted to human rights in the context of the fight against terrorism fortunately ends with reference to the work of parliament on the cia flights and extraordinary renditions, but it says nothing about the council's inaction in terms of continuing the investigations, bringing those responsible to justice and even less about compensating the victims who have been unjustly transferred, imprisoned or tortured. similarly, the chapter on asylum and migration is silent on the massive violations of the rights of migrants; on behalf of the ind/dem group. dear colleagues, 'a new man of human rights has been born who has only the name in common with his ancestor of 1789', these are the words in which the philosopher marcel gauchet sums up the charter of fundamental rights which has just been proclaimed here and to which article 6 of the treaty of lisbon gives binding force. in many respects, as we know, the many rights it enshrines contradict the rights and freedoms protected by our national constitutions. european law is superior to national law, even constitutional law. what, then, is left of the principle of secularism in the face of article 10 of the charter, which states that freedom of religion implies freedom to manifest one's religion in private and in public? what will remain of the principle of equality in the face of articles 20 et seq. of the charter, which list victims' rights based on group membership? what is left of the principle of freedom, which is a right to self-determination, in the face of articles 6 to 19, which confuse it with rights of claim, the mere power to demand a benefit from others? we would like to accelerate the transformation of the citizen from an actor into a vulgar consumer, a passive provider of services, which is the only way to do it! to those of my colleagues who would be attached to the centuries-old rights and freedoms of their nation, protected by their constitution, i say only one word: wake up!
mr president, i am grateful for this report, but would like to point out that our human rights are still selective – they are politically correct. even in this house we could not hold a photographic exhibition on the atrocities in chechnya, because we were afraid that the russians would not like it. concerning our human rights dialogue with china, there was no mention of the 30 to 40 million girls who are missing, demographically-speaking, in china. where are those children? they have been aborted, murdered after birth or abandoned, or are in the hands of organised crime. therefore, next time, our mission should be to take up this matter with the chinese authorities. are things any better in the eu? i by no means want to make anyone feel guilty. all i am asking is for you to consider what the basis of humanity is. why do we point a finger – quite rightly – at those countries which have the death sentence when we also have a death sentence in the eu, with over one million children in the eu being murdered before they can be born? all i am asking is whether this is humane. can we build a sounder society when human life does not have an absolute value? our first mission is to defend the defenceless, those who are the most vulnerable. that is called real solidarity. this may not be politically correct thinking, but we have to ask where the values lie. are they negotiable? can human rights values depend on a majority reached one day, which may be a minority another day? to put it simply, the first human right is to be born. i am very happy i was born, and i am sure my colleagues are happy that they were born. by seeing the absolute value of human life, we can build a society of compassion and love. we cannot build a better tomorrow on sand that is wet from the tears of unborn children.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on legal affairs of the european parliament has approved, after some amendments, the proposal for a directive on the legal protection of designs. i regret that the text adopted provides, in the very short term, for the abolition of protection for designs, particularly for visible body parts of cars. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive on the protection of consumers in the event of a serious accident. the european union regularly stresses the decisive role of intellectual property protection for the competitiveness of enterprises. for many years the institutions and the member states have been working to promote the adoption of community rules on intellectual property in the internal market. the present proposal is in total contradiction with this policy and will open a major breach in the community's protection of industrial property rights. this protection should not be denied to automobile spare parts or to many other complex products which are the result of original artistic creativity and considerable investment. contrary to what is claimed, but never established, the removal of protection for car spare parts would not bring any benefits to consumers. the benefit to the final consumer is not shown in terms of price/quality ratio. in fact, a study commissioned by the european commission shows that full liberalisation of the car parts market would not necessarily benefit consumers in terms of prices because of the number of intermediaries between suppliers of spare parts and the final consumer. the abolition of protection would in reality benefit only economic operators who would not have to bear the costs of creation and would not, unlike manufacturers who have to look after their image, have the same concern to respect the characteristics which the buyer believes he can expect from the product. the european commission's proposal could therefore encourage the production of lower quality spare parts or even indirectly encourage counterfeiting. for all these reasons, i regret the position adopted by the commission, and i have said so and i continue to support the two amendments tabled by myself and 50 of my colleagues which provide for a transitional period of eight years for the protection of designs.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's proposal is intended to allow companies other than manufacturers to manufacture spare parts and, in so doing, to reduce the price of parts and insurance. this is the idyllic presentation which was made to us a moment ago by the commissioner for the internal market. there is no evidence that these benefits for consumers will be real. the countries that have removed protection have not seen any obvious progress. the commission's own studies confirm this, and our rapporteur, klaus-heiner lehne, has just told us so. on the other hand, the abolition of intellectual property rights in many industries, not just the automobile sector, is directly contrary to the economic and commercial strategy of the european union. it is opening the door to counterfeiting, it is giving dangerous competitors, such as china or india, the opportunity to go into rampant production of these materials. this is the exact opposite of the lisbon strategy, which sought to make intellectual property the weapon of competitiveness and innovation. we would be giving our competitors the opposite signal to this strategy and that would be contrary to europe's interests in the context of globalisation. in the end, ladies and gentlemen, this proposal is out of date. it is based on an ideological approach which, in 2007, is completely wrong, given that we are now engaged in a vital battle with the new economic giants for survival in our industry. this is no time to disarm! commissioner mandelson is going to beijing to force china to respect intellectual property and here, at the same time, we are questioning it. in sum, this proposal should be simply abandoned as unrealistic and irresponsible. now that we are engaged in the debate, we must behave like good legislators. that is why, at the very least, we support the rapporteur's compromise and call on our assembly to vote in favour of the amendment signed by 53 members and which provides for an eight-year transition period.

in writing. in the lehne report on the legal protection of designs, i decided to support and co-sign an amendment proposing an eight-year transitional period before a global liberalisation of intellectual property rights on spare parts which are used to give the original appearance to complex products, such as motor vehicles. at present, the impact studies have not shown a significant price decrease for these parts for consumers in the member states where liberalisation has been achieved. moreover, it seems to me that the european union is acting against its interests in this matter. other parts of the world are protecting their industry with industrial property rights and the european union, which is also showing its will to protect consumers and to fight against counterfeiting, is not making the right choice here. the economic equilibrium of the automobile sector and the safety of european citizens are at stake.
in writing. the proposed directive on the legal protection of designs proposes the total liberalisation of the market for spare parts, particularly in the automobile sector. the rapporteur's text largely modifies this proposal by introducing, in particular, the possibility for member states to maintain their legislation on strict design protection for another five years. by preserving the manufacturers' monopoly on the manufacture of spare parts, the aim is to avoid the relocation of community jobs to countries such as turkey, brazil or korea, where production is carried out at lower costs and with lower quality. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the free movement of goods between the european community and the republic of south africa. since spare parts are manufactured without any responsibility on the part of the car manufacturers, there is no a priori guarantee of the conformity or quality of the spare parts. the main objective must be to protect and safeguard users, above all economic and political considerations. after the postal services, railways, energy and electricity, brussels is now tackling the car industry. the logic of ultra-globalist and ideologically driven liberalisation knows no bounds. member of the commission. mr president, once again we have the opportunity to discuss this serious health threat in the european parliament. it was only a few months ago that we had the opportunity to discuss the community action plan regarding this health threat. our concern does not, of course, relate only to the european community, but also to the whole world. we are concerned with the rise of infections, with the number of people who are affected and living with hiv worldwide, and the number of 33 million people, for us, is too high. therefore, we want to take action within the european union but also coordinate with all the other international players outside the eu to tackle this issue globally. this also matches the new european community health strategy, which includes a global role for the european union in the area of health. areas we can concentrate on: first of all, to prevent infection – this is very important. at the same time, to make sure that testing is available, and treatment and care where needed. to achieve all this, we need to raise awareness, and this is a very important factor; this is something where we are lagging behind – i will come back to that in a minute. but also the social stigma. this is one of our major concerns, and in a way this works as a vicious circle, because the social stigma prevents people from wanting to test themselves and learning whether they have been infected, and therefore, they could infect others. they do not seek treatment and do not get tested, with all the negative effects. this is more worrying among young people, and this is our main concern and target. our studies and polls show that, among young people, there really is a lack of knowledge – one could say there is ignorance when it comes to these health threats. so it is important to show to them in a balanced way, in a way that presents information and on the one hand does not create panic but on the other hand does not lead to complacency, that it is a serious disease; there is no cure for it, but they can protect themselves – and they can be shown how to do that – and at the same time that they should not be afraid of fellow citizens who have the infection, who have the disease. we have seen two extremes from the eurobarometer. some young people think that there is nothing to worry about: you take some antibiotics and it goes away. on the other hand, just by touching infected people or even sharing a glass with them or through a kiss one can catch the disease. so we see two extreme views regarding this health threat, and neither deals effectively with our aim, which is to control the spread and further infections. world aids day is an important day and gives us an opportunity to discuss and raise awareness; but we should not limit ourselves to this one day, and that is why i am happy that, within the european union at least, we will be discussing these issues continuously. but when it comes to young people, we have to remind ourselves that we had very active, very effective, very aggressive campaigns in the 1980s which managed to reach the goal of raising awareness, but then we stopped and we forgot that a young generation, a new generation of young people became sexually active after the end of those campaigns. in fact, some of them were born just before the end of those campaigns, and they did not and discussions with young people, understanding, first of all, what they know or do not know about this disease, and also some practical problems. they know, for example, that the use of condoms is the best protection, but at the same time, how can they get them? they are too embarrassed or they are worried or they are shy. so we see some practical effects that we never thought were problems, never thought we would have to face in europe. but they are still there. also, because we want to talk to young people in language that they understand, the commission this year took the initiative of producing a new tv spot addressing the prevention of hiv transmission. this was done through a competition among young people, and the best one chosen, the winning entry, was by a polish student. we produced that, and it was broadcast by several tv channels and was also used in the school visits. this is an important strategy which we must follow: we have to talk to young people in the language they understand. but, as i said earlier, the challenges arising from hiv and aids are present well beyond the european union boundaries. it is true that, worldwide, there has been some good progress in terms of access to hiv-related services, especially low-middle-income countries. now, about 95% of people infected with hiv live in those countries. thanks to an unprecedented increase in international funding in these countries, the number of people receiving treatment has considerably increased, from 100 000 in 2001 to 2.5 million people in 2007. these are impressive figures; nevertheless, more than 70% of people in need of arv treatment in these countries do not receive it or do not have access to it. this shows that we still have a long way to go. the european action is financed through a wide array of financial instruments both at national and global level, such as the global fund, for example. there are also other financing mechanisms through public private partnerships. progress has been achieved through these joint efforts with the international community, but we still have a long way to go, and this requires strong cooperation among the european institutions. as i said at the beginning, our principal goal is to bring the number of new hiv infections down and work towards the best possible solutions in terms of support, treatment and care for those who are already living with hiv/aids. i therefore want to emphasis this once again: fighting the stigma – the social exclusion, the discrimination of the disease and people suffering from it or the necessary actions. in this respect i am counting – and i know i have it – on the support of the european parliament.

a system where many market players are cross-border players, or with deposit guarantee schemes which are not at least harmonised or, at any rate, developed on the same basis, and this is due to competition but also to trust in market mechanisms. i was very struck, during my various trips this summer, which did not concern only the nordic countries, by the question of the guarantee system, which was systematically put to me as a crucial question. of course, i know the answer from the commissioner's services, which is to say: 'but, after all, if you add up all the guarantee systems at european level, you have only a tiny fraction of the sums needed to deal with crises.' this is not a sufficient argument to respond to the handicap in terms of competition and in terms of confidence in the market mechanisms, especially since it leads to perverse effects in the strategy of companies which, as a result, arbitrate between subsidiaries and branches on the basis of the wrong reasons. with all these elements in mind, i asked my group for support. my group tabled an amendment asking the commission to speed up its work and to take account of the expectations of the citizens, who do not express this as a priority and strong demand, but who ask to be reassured about the mechanisms of the european financial markets and the correctness of their mode of intervention. a good deposit guarantee system at european level could only help. i believe, commissioner, that it is your responsibility to assess the state of confidence in the functioning of financial markets at european level. it seems to me that we cannot simply wait for further studies in this respect. you must make things happen faster and we can move forward on a more harmonized basis, with a more transparent and clearer reading of the deposit guarantee mechanisms as they operate at the level of the european union.
madam president, commissioner, i thank the rapporteur for his text. in this document we deal with recurring topics. for example, what are the barriers between institutional, professional, and private investors? some people want to believe that there is some sort of "great wall of china" between the two. i don't believe it, and recent events have shown us how financial innovation spreads from class to class and eventually reaches the final saver. so the fiction of legislation which is entirely built on the existence of two types of investors - informed and professional investors on the one hand and investors who are small savers on the other - is in my view dangerous. there is a gradual shift in products and we know it well. that notion may exist but we must deal with it with lucidity. the second point i would like to raise, which is also found in other texts on financial markets, is that of investor information. of course, it is essential that everything is done about it because the complexity of financial innovation is a new element that has not been taken into account and has not been addressed until now. but that is not enough, it cannot replace the responsibility of the distributors of products and i think that needs to be recalled. thirdly, commissioner, i think you have failed to articulate the implementation of the mifid directive with the ucits directive. is it normal that mifid has been implemented in the member states even before its articulation with the ucits directive is known? i think we would be in a better balance if it had been otherwise. the rapporteur referred to the taxation issue in terms of merging funds. i think that we should not forget the problems also in terms of product placement, which can be hampered by obstacles of a purely fiscal nature. finally, i would like to come to the socialist amendment, because the reality of the market for these products is not the same depending on whether one is addressing a country which produces such products, a country which consumes them or a country which is both a producer and a consumer. we have introduced the idea of reciprocity which would not only apply to the opening up or access to markets, but also to the nature of regulation and supervision. i think this is an absolutely essential element because the idea that a country outside the european union which only produces such products could access our markets on any terms on the grounds that we would have access to its market, when it would not be of interest to any european consumer, does not seem to me realistic, or it seems to me a theoretical argument which is not acceptable. the rapporteur sometimes tells us that reciprocity would be contrary to wto rules. but, commissioner, what did we do when we agreed to rules of equivalence with the united states? that's exactly what we're asking you to use here. finally, this would not be realistic, since we would not have harmonisation within the european union. well, if the negotiation of equivalence with third countries could lead us to define a common level of regulation and supervision within the european union, i think we would have made very great progress.
mr president, on this point i agree with what mr corbett has said. i would just like to add that i was here this morning at the sitting to hear the group chairman, mr bonde, apologise for what happened yesterday to the bailiffs. what is unacceptable is that we are attacking, with words or phrases, i would not even say too strong, but frankly disgusting - excuse me for the term, but i use the same language - the staff of our parliament, which has only done its duty as the president and the presidency asked it to do. i see that there is no official apology, so we will have to take the necessary measures to defend the staff of parliament. that's why i'm here this morning.
mr president, commissioner, two years ago, following the lifting of quotas, the textile sector experienced a real big bang. to try to remedy this crisis, you, mr commissioner, are advocating transitional but palliative measures, with the ambition of controlling and limiting imports of certain chinese textiles. in a few days' time these safeguards will no longer exist and trade in textiles will be subject to the watch of a european union-china joint eye, which i hope will be attentive and vigilant. our concern today is how this joint surveillance system will be put in place. what guarantees do we have to ensure that this double control will be adequate and effective? the textile sector has always been a globalist sector in terms of both production and consumption, but it has suffered the consequences of a certain degree of globalisation. but this globalisation can be anticipated and regulated. this requires the political will to create a competitive environment for our european textile industries. we must move towards fair and reciprocal market access conditions. we must continue to use the trade defence instruments at the disposal of the european union without fear, because protectionism is not protectionism. we must make the fight against counterfeiting our priority. the europe of tomorrow will not have any industry if we do not defend its intellectual property rights and know-how. the application of the same rules of the game by all and for all is the only way to offer all parties involved a win-win scenario. i therefore hope that in 2008, mr mandelson, we can look together in a more serene atmosphere at the promising future of the textile sector.
president. - ladies and gentlemen, with just a few weeks to go until the end of the negotiations on the memorandum of understanding providing for restrictions on imports of chinese textiles, it is essential that the european parliament adopt a strong position on the future of its textile sector, whose structures and methods of organization are threatened by brutal competition with china. the joint resolution we are proposing today calls for a clear commitment from the european commission and the member states on several points. firstly, to ensure that the enterprises and workers in the sector, which are facing the risk of major restructuring, are fully supported by adequate social measures and by the allocation of european funds to support the modernisation of their production structures. secondly, we must work to strengthen the competitiveness of the european textile sector within the broader framework of a strong and ambitious european industrial policy. this objective cannot be achieved unless we turn words into action and invest heavily in research and development. moreover, faced with unfair competition from some of our competitors, who base their comparative advantages on social or environmental dumping or both, europe needs effective trade defence instruments. this greater efficiency will not be achieved by hasty reform, which would weaken the union's means of protection, but by a more transparent and predictable use of existing instruments. finally, europe must make the euro-mediterranean partnership the foundation of an integrated production area which takes advantage of the proximity of the mediterranean countries to be more competitive on the international textile market. the development of the mediterranean countries with which we wish to establish a stronger partnership depends on our ability to offer them concrete commitments on policies and areas of activity of common interest.
mr president, when i spoke in this house on the same subject in july 2005, i said that the lessons we would learn from the textile crisis would ultimately help us to maintain and develop other sectors of the european economy. i think we've made some progress, but not much. we are always calling for more research and development and for the commission to ensure that intellectual property is respected. these are important but not sufficient factors. i am thinking that instead of being a factor for increased trade and economic development, the wto and its rules are a brake. trade is obviously a source of growth, but to do so it must go both ways. the textile question reflects two fundamental problems: the absence of an industrial policy in the union and the question of the european interest. as regards the european interest, i welcome the commission communication entitled 'the european interest: meeting the challenge of globalisation' published at the beginning of october, which states that 'our basic rules must not compromise our ability to protect our interests or our ability to maintain the high standards we apply to products to ensure the protection of health, safety, the environment and consumers'. we will not tolerate third countries wishing to operate in the european union circumventing the rules applied in the internal market. commissioner, let us start by applying these principles to the textile industry!

in writing. the paradox, if not the entire hypocrisy of the european parliament, is that it loudly proclaims democratic principles and values while largely flouting them by refusing to apply them when it does not suit it. this was the case yesterday when the european parliament, meeting in plenary, solemnly proclaimed the charter of fundamental rights in a general chaos, thus ignoring the objections from the sovereignist benches who were calling for a referendum on the adoption of the new constitutional treaty. the european parliament discredits itself by refusing to discuss and by stigmatising its own elected representatives who are concerned with the preservation of national identity and sovereignty. freedom of expression is only valuable if political opponents can also benefit from it. the right-thinking political groups seem to think that there is an illegitimate speech that must be prevented at all costs. while parliament is committing itself by demanding the charter of fundamental rights, the elected representatives of the national front are loudly reaffirming that they do not share the same conception of human rights and that they will continue their fight for respect for the sovereignty and identity of the nations of europe.
in writing. the national front, vlaams belang and fpoe are not extremist, racist or xenophobic parties. in a spirit of unhealthy and false amalgamation, all the so-called "well-thinking" parties are endeavouring to brand them as extremists simply because they are concerned with promoting the preservation of national identity. democracy is in danger, but the culprits pre-designated by the system are not the right ones. it is not those who criticize and challenge policies, especially immigration, who are accused of being extremists. no, it is those who systematically muzzle freedom of expression in the name of human rights and political correctness and who in reality only mask their failures to solve the immigration, insecurity and identity issues they face. by increasing the number of laws to combat extremism in europe, parliament could have taken pride in its contribution to the maintenance of democratic principles and values. unfortunately, this is not the case, and far from targeting radical islamism or totalitarian communist regimes, parliament is once again indulging its anti-national and globalist obsession.
in writing. it is astonishing how hemiplegic the european parliament can be: it only looks to the right! the various resolutions proposed by the pse, the liberals, the greens and the communists only consider extremism from the 'far right' point of view. what about radical islamists and trotskyists and communists of all stripes? not once are these extremes targeted. it is an insult to all the victims of totalitarian communist regimes and to all those who suffer daily from the dogmas and practices of radical islam. the european parliament does not condemn these extremes. they simply do not exist because they do not participate in the standard terminology of political correctness that is in force in this chamber. in a spirit of respect for the principles and values of democracy, equality and tolerance, the socialist group does not hesitate to 'welcome the dissolution of the far-right group independence, tradition and sovereignty' before calling for stricter conditions governing the formation of political groups in parliament. the leitmotif of these elected officials is to systematically demonize their political opponents in order to impose their well-thought-out thinking on everyone. these resolutions are thoughts of hypocrisy, blindness and obscurantism. we will vote against it.

in writing. the textile sector in france and europe since the end of the multifibre arrangement has turned some of our regions into economic and social deserts. there is now precariousness and poverty for thousands of women and men who have lost their jobs. the destruction of these enterprises, of this social fabric, in the name of globalisation and europeanist ultra-liberalism, is the symbol of one of the european union's greatest economic failures. for years this logic has led to the relocation of our production, even of the best quality, in all other economic sectors to other countries in the world: north africa and especially asia. this global rebalancing has in reality brought nothing to third countries, except the aggravation of economic slavery for the benefit of a small elite within the chinese factory and the permanent establishment of unemployment in europe against the background of a persistent economic crisis. it is clear that the global competition encouraged by the wto is the main reason for the widespread impoverishment and lack of european dynamism. it is urgent that the european union should put an end to this madness and finally put in place community protection and preference.
